## Opening the necessary input and output files

FVS needs to open various input and output files that are required in a projection and establish database connections if stand or tree data is coming from a database. When the keyword record file name is not specified as a command line option, FVS will prompt users for 6 file names. These names can be provided via keyboard input or the names can be supplied in a response file. When running FVS through the Suppose interface, Suppose builds a batch file and runs FVS via DOS commands and supplies the answers to the prompts. If run from FVSOnline, a new FVS interface (code is at https://sourceforge.net/p/open-fvs/code/HEAD/tree/rFVS/shinyFVSOnline/ and more information is at https://sourceforge.net/p/open-fvs/wiki/FVSOnline/), command line options are used to specify input file names.

The first file opened is the file containing FVS keyword records, referred to as the “keyword record file” (or simply “keyword file”). A keyword record file is required to make an FVS projection. A detailed description of the keyword record file can be found in section 4.1 of the EFVS guide. How FVS reads this file will be discussed in sections 3.3 and 3.4 of this document.

If needed, the second file opened is a file containing individual tree data records, referred to as the “tree data file”. A detailed description of the tree data file is provided in section 4.2 of the EFVS guide.  A tree data file is not required when making a bare ground simulation or when all of the tree data will be read from a database table. In these instances, the file name “NUL” (or /dev/null on Unix-like platforms) should be specified for the tree data file name if FVS prompts for it. In a bare ground simulation the NOTREES keyword record must also be included as one of the keyword records in the keyword record file.

The next four prompts are for output file names. The third prompt is for the main FVS output file; the fourth for the tree list output file (requested with the TREELIST keyword record); the fifth is for the summary output file (requested with the ECHOSUM keyword record); and the sixth is for an auxiliary file used for input to post-processing programs like CHEAPOII. Default file names exist for these files if the user enters “NUL” or a blank when FVS prompts for these file names. Detailed descriptions of these output files are provided in section 4.3 of the EFVS guide. In multi-stand runs, output from all stands included in the keyword record file will be written to these files. When you enter the name of the keyword record file on the command line, FVS does not prompt for these file names. It automatically creates the files if and when they are needed by replacing the suffix of the keyword record file name (generally, “.key”) with other suffices, as follows: “.out” for the output, “.trl” for tree list, “.chp” for the CHEAPOII file, and “.tre” for the input tree list (see table 3-2).

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine fvsSetCmdLine (source code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) which then calls subroutine GENRPT to initialize the multiple report file. The multiple report file is a scratch file that FVS uses to temporarily store information that will eventually end up in the main output file. Information for several output reports is written to this file as the output is computed along with a report number identifying which output report the information will eventually go to. At the end of a simulation of each stand, all the reports will be written to the FVS output files in proper projection sequence. If there are over 200 different reports saved in the file, then the file is converted to a permanent file and saved for post-projection processing.

Subroutine fvsSetCmdLine (source code contained in subroutine CMDLINE) then calls subroutine FILOPN to open the keyword record file and the output file.  The tree data file and other FVS output files are opened when, and if, they are needed. Subroutine FILOPN sets up the file specification parameters and issues OPEN commands or calls subroutine MYOPEN to open files. FILOPN prompts for file names when the name of the keyword record file is not specified on the command line. When the keyword record file is specified on the command line, the names of other needed files are automatically formed using the keyword record file prefix as the common prefix, and suffices as listed in table 3-2.

Programmers need to be aware that subroutine MYOPEN once contained operating-system dependent code that needed to be modified for different operating environments. However, since about 2005, FVS is being coded using modern FORTRAN standards, so the need for this operating-system dependent code has evaporated and MYOPEN should therefore be phased out. In some of the more recent code its use has been avoided.

Sometime in the early 2000s, a new file handling subroutine was added called “openIfClosed” (the source code for this subroutine is part of the source code of subroutine FILOPN). An example using this code is in subroutine PRTRLS, the subroutine that writes the tree list output table. Subroutine openIfClosed is called prior to writing to the designed unit number. It checks to see if the file is opened, and opens it if it is not. It always opens a file with POSITION=’append’, so if a fresh file is desired, the old one needs to be discarded prior to the run starting. The assigned file name is the prefix name of the keyword record file and the suffix that is passed to subroutine openIfClosed (in the case of the tree list, the suffix is “.trl” as shown in table 3-2). This strategy was introduced so FVS does not create many unused empty files that need to be deleted later. It also simplified the coding of the stop/restart capability (section 8.0) because the upper-level programming code need not open files until, and unless, they are actually needed for output.

A unit number is associated with each file. Those used by the FVS base model are specified in subroutine BLKDAT; those used in the regeneration establishment extension can be found in subroutine ESBLKD; those associated with other extensions can be found in various other places. Table 3-1 shows unit numbers and associated variable names that are used for some purpose in FVS. Programmers should avoid using these unit numbers for any other purpose in FVS when adding new features to the model. Furthermore, there is a capability in modern FORTRAN that provides a file unit number for use. An example of its use is in the Climate-FVS extension’s CLIN subroutine where the OPEN statement uses the NEWUNIT feature of the FORTRAN OPEN statement. This construct should replace the fixed unit assignments for many files listed in table 3-1. Unit 30 associated with variable KOLIST is a good example of where the OPEN(NEWUNIT =…) construct could easily replace the unit assignment, and should be changed.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Various other subroutines serve minor, but either necessary or nice, roles in this process.

Subroutine REVISE is used to retrieve the variants last revision date. This is used, along with the 2-character unique alpha variant code, to label FVS output files.

Subroutine UNBLNK is used to remove blanks from a character string, leaving the nonblank contents of the string left justified in the string and the rest of the string blank. It also returns the length of the nonblank portion of the string.

Subroutine RCDSET is used to set the FVS error severity value (10, 20, or 30) and is called from several places in the program. It has two arguments, the second indicates if the error warrants ending the run. This case, when the call is from subroutine FILOPN, will cause FVS to end processing when the keyword record file is not present and there is no restart file (see section 8). FVS requires a keyword record file to set the projection parameters, specifications, and management activities. If a keyword record file is not present and there is no restart file, the run will stop.

KEYFN, an entry point in subroutine KEYRDR, is used to save the keyword record file name from subroutine FILOPN for writing to the output file. This feature documents the name of the keyword record file that was used to create the run, in the output file. It is also used when automatic filenames are generated in the case where the keyword record file is input on the command line. Lastly, this name is added to the CASES table of the database output and is used to relate all the output tables in the database that were created from a single FVS run. A case is a single run of a single stand as defined in the database extension documentation (Crookston and others 2003).

## Initializing parameters to their starting values

FVS needs to initialize all model parameters to their starting values. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine INITRE to accomplish this task. In multi-stand runs this is the point to which control transfers at the beginning each stand in the run.

The goal upon completion of this task is that every model control parameter needed for the FVS projection of the individual stand will have a value. The value may be the model’s default value or a value set by the user, but all parameters will have a value. This is accomplished in three steps: 1) default values are assigned to all model control parameters; 2) keyword records are processed and user specified values replace some of the default values; and 3) default values for parameters that were not set by the user, but are dependent on other parameter values set by the user, are assigned.

### Subroutines involved and their function

For step 1, subroutine INITRE calls subroutine GRINIT to set the default conditions for the beginning of the simulation for a stand. Subroutine GRINIT contains variant-specific initializations for many model variables, including those variables that are either species-specific, used for output summarization, or stand-specific such as slope, aspect, and elevation.

Step 2, processing of the keyword records, is done by subroutine INITRE along with the help of many other subroutines. This will be explained in greater detail in the next section.

For step 3, subroutine INITRE calls subroutine SITSET that is another variant-specific subroutine. The role of subroutine SITSET is to make sure those model control parameters that may be dependent on other parameter settings, all have a value. Examples are species-specific site index values or stand density index values where the user may have set values for a few, but not all, species recognized by the variant.

### Auxiliary subroutines

The purpose of this document is to describe the program flow during model execution. However, from a programmer’s perspective it is worth mentioning there are other FVS subroutines involved in model initialization. Some are base model subroutines where values are loaded at compile time rather than run time.

Subroutine BLKDAT is a variant-specific BLOCK DATA subroutine that contains base model parameter settings such as the species codes the variant recognizes. These are all set with DATA statements and loaded at compile time. Other variant-specific and base model subroutines contain DATA statements that load default equation coefficients and model parameters at compile time.

Subroutine ESBLKD is another BLOCK DATA subroutine that contains regeneration establishment extension settings that are loaded at compile time. These settings are not variant-specific.

Various other extensions have their own initialization subroutines. Some have DATA statements that load at compile time, while others like subroutine FMINIT for the fire and fuels extension load at run time. Some of these, like subroutine FMINIT, are extension specific and some are variant-specific, like subroutine MISINTCR for the mistletoe extension in the Central Rockies variant. Initialization subroutines for the various base model extensions include: ESINIT, MPBINT, DFBINT, TMINIT, BWEINT, CVINIT, RDINIT, MISIN0, MISINT, BRINIT, ISSTAG, FMINIT, SVINIT, BGCINT, ECINIT, DBSINIT, and CLINIT.

And finally, the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP), contain a section of code in subroutine GRINIT to initialize variables needed to run the ORGANON subroutines. These variables also load at run time. Structural differences of the ORGANON-FVS variants will be further discussed in section 9.0.

## Processing keyword record requests

Users communicate run control information to FVS through the use of keyword records. Consequently, use of the keyword record system is described throughout the EFVS guide and is the basis of FVS training sessions and tutorials. Keyword record processing is echoed to the main FVS output file unless a user turns this feature off with the NOECHO keyword record.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine INITRE orchestrates the processing of all keyword records. If the PARMS format, discussed in section 6.1 of the EFVS guide, is not being used, subroutine INITRE also checks the keyword record parameter fields for valid values and assigns default parameter values if some of the parameter values are missing. If values for required parameter fields are missing, or if supplied values are incorrect, then the keyword record is rejected. In this case, subroutine KEYDMP is called to echo the keyword record to the FVS main output file and subroutine ERRGRO is called to write an error message to the FVS main output file giving the user some idea of what problem was encountered. Processing then continues with the next keyword record. If the PARMS format is being used, parameter field checking is not done.

Keyword records convey different types of information to FVS and are dealt with in different ways. Keyword records may be used to set constants, schedule management activities, or serve as flags to indicate program control needs to be temporarily transferred to a different part of FVS, such as one of the FVS extensions, for processing to continue.

#### Keyword records that can be dealt with once

Some keyword records can be dealt with once and then FVS is done with them for the simulation of a particular stand. Keyword records that simply convey parameter settings FVS should use instead of the model default values are of this type. Examples of these are the BAMAX keyword record that sets the biological basal area maximum for the stand and the DEFECT keyword record that sets species-specific defect corrections for volume estimates. Keyword records that allow users to enter equation coefficients are also of this type. An example is the CWEQN keyword record that allows users to enter their own species-specific crown width equation coefficients.

In both of these cases subroutine INITRE directly stores the new parameter values in the appropriate variable or array, echoes the information to the output file unless keyword record echoing is turned off, and FVS is done with processing that particular keyword record request.

#### Keyword records that transfer control to another part of FVS for processing

A special case of keyword records that can be dealt with once in FVS by subroutine INITRE are those that transfer control to another keyword record processing subroutine within the FVS structure. Examples are the COMPUTE keyword record that transfers control to the event monitor subroutine EVUSRV, and the FMIN keyword record that transfers control to the fire and fuels extension keyword record processing subroutine FMIN.

Control remains in the location outside of subroutine INITRE until an END keyword record is encountered at which time control returns to subroutine INITRE. Any keyword records encountered between these special signal keyword records are processed by the designated components of FVS. Some of these between keyword records will be handled directly by the receiving subroutine as discussed above, and some will be scheduled as discussed below. In either case, keyword records are handled in the same way as discussed for subroutine INITRE base model keyword record processing, with one exception. Processing of event monitor instructions is quite different and will be discussed in section 3.4. Subroutines that process extension specific keyword records include: BGCIN, BMPPIN, BRIN, BWEIN, CVIN, CLIN, DATABASE, DFBIN, DFTMIN, ESIN, FMIN, MISIN, MPBIN, ORIN, and RDIN.

#### Keyword records that need to be scheduled

Many FVS model instructions can be issued by year (often called “date”) or projection cycle. Examples are management activities such as thinning requests and model multipliers that alter predicted model outputs. Instructions of this type must be handled by the option processing subroutines within FVS that posts the instructions to the activity schedule table and then retrieves them at the appropriate time by the appropriate portion of the FVS code for implementation. Most keyword records of this type support the PARMS format discussed in section 6.1 of the EFVS guide. For some, like the TREELIST keyword record, the PARMS format would not make sense and is not supported; there aren’t any parameter fields on the TREELIST keyword record that are dynamic. How FVS processes the PARMS format is discussed in section 3.4.3.

3.3.1.3.1 Scheduling the Option

Subroutine INITRE calls subroutine KEYRDR to read a keyword record. That subroutine (which is also used by the extensions) checks the parameter fields if the PARMS format is not being used. If the checks are satisfied, subroutine OPNEW is called to post the activity to the activity schedule table. If the PARMS format is in use, parameter fields are not checked and subroutine OPNEWC is called to post the activity to the activity schedule table. In either case, a unique option code (also called an activity number) is associated with each activity. Information posted to the activity schedule includes the unique option code, the year the activity is being scheduled, and the parameters associated with the activity. Option codes associated with FVS keyword records are shown in subroutine OPLIST (see section 6.0).

3.3.1.3.2 Retrieving and Processing the Option

It is the responsibility of individual subroutines pertaining to the activity to check the activity schedule, retrieve any activities posted there for the current cycle, and process the information contained in the associated parameters. For example, it is the responsibility of subroutine CUTS to retrieve any thinning-related activities from the activity schedule each projection cycle. The processing subroutine, in this example CUTS, contains a list of unique option codes it is responsible for processing. This list is typically stored in a local array called MYACTS(i). Subroutine OPFIND is called to see if any activities on the activity schedule for the current cycle match those in the list. If there are, then OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called for each of the scheduled activities to retrieve the parameters associated with the activity. These activities are returned in the order they are scheduled (the year), or, when activities are scheduled in the same year, then in the order they were specified. The processing subroutine then stores the associated parameters in the appropriate variables for processing. OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to post the activity and its disposition to the activity summary. Possible dispositions include “DONE”, “NOT DONE”, or “DELETED OR CANCELLED”.

“DONE” means the activity was processed successfully.

“NOT DONE” usually means there was an error at some point in processing the keyword record. With improvements in keyword record parameter checking and defaulting, it is extremely rare to encounter this disposition for this reason. Other reasons an activity would get marked “NOT DONE” are that the activity was posted to occur in a year that is not within the time scope of the simulation; or it was dynamically posted for a year that has already past in simulation time. In those cases, the activity is simply never explicitly considered. Lastly, a “NOT DONE” can be seen when a programmer has failed to include a call to OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, where one should exist.

“DELETED OR CANCELLED” means the activity was considered but parameter settings could not be satisfied. For example, if a diameter limit thinning in the DBH range 0.0” – 5.0” was specified for cycle 3, and there were no trees in the stand with diameters less than 5.0” in cycle 3, then this diameter limit thinning request would be “DELETED OR CANCELLED”.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutines used in reading event monitor instructions will be discussed in section 3.4.

Subroutine DUNN is a variant-specific subroutine that translates Dunning site codes to regular site index values. Dunning site codes are valid for FVS variants used in Forest Service Region 5 and may be entered using the SITECODE keyword record.

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine FFIN is used to process parameters on the FERTILIZ keyword record and schedule the fertilization activity.

Subroutine FNDKEY is used to find a keyword record name in the keyword record name table. FVS base model keyword record names are in an array called TABLE(i) which is loaded in the BLOCK DATA code segment KEYWDS, and carried in the KEYCOM labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine FORKOD is used to translate the forest code entered on the STDINFO keyword record into a subscript that is stored in variable IFOR and used to index forest specific growth constants or coefficients in various parts of FVS. If the forest code is missing, or invalid, a default value is assigned. The actual forest code corresponding to the forest index is stored in variable KODFOR. Both IFOR and KODFOR are stored in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine GETSED is called to generate a seed value for the FVS random number generator. The seed value is passed to RANSED, an entry point in subroutine RANN, to reseed the random number generator.

Subroutine HABTYP is used to translate the habitat type entered on the STDINFO keyword record into a subscript that is stored in variable ITYPE and used to index habitat specific growth constants or coefficients in various parts of FVS. If the habitat type is missing, or invalid, a default value is assigned. The actual habitat type corresponding to the habitat type index is stored in variable KODTYP.  Both ITYPE and KODTYP are stored in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine KEYDMP writes a keyword record to the main output file when the parameter values contain errors severe enough that the keyword record is being rejected.

Subroutine KEYOPN opens an external file for input or output as requested with the OPEN keyword record.

Subroutine KEYRDR is used to read the FVS base model keyword records. Keyword records are read in both character and real formats. Keyword records are decoded and scanned for the PARMS format. If a STOP keyword record is encountered, subroutine KEYRDR calls GRSTOP, an entry point in subroutine ERRGRO, to close database connections, close any open file units, set an appropriate return code, and return back to subroutine FVS.

Subroutine KSSTAG is called to process parameters associated with structural call calculations entered with the STRCLASS keyword record.

Subroutine LBAGLR is used to read the activity group label for the current activity group entered with the AGPLABEL keyword record.

Subroutine LBDSET writes the default stand label set to the FVS main output table and assigns the stand label set to all activity groups for which no activity group label set has been specified.

Subroutine LBSPLR is used to read the stand policy label set entered with the SPLABEL keyword record.

Subroutine SDEFLN is called to process parameters associated with the BFFDLN and MCFDLN keyword records that are used to set species-specific defect coefficients for volume calculations.

Subroutine SDEFET is called to schedule activities associated with the MCDEFECT and BFDEFECT keyword records. These keyword records are used to enter species-specific defect correction factors used in volume calculations.

Subroutine SPDECD decodes the species code for keyword records that contain species-specific parameters. The species code entered on the keyword record may be the FVS species sequence number, the FVS alpha species code, the species group name, or a value of zero indicating the parameters apply to all species.

Subroutine SVKEY is called to process parameters associated with the Stand Visualization System and entered with the SVS keyword record.

Subroutine TRNASP translates the aspect in degrees entered on the STDINFO keyword record to a value in radians by multiplying the degree aspect by the constant 0.0174533. The translated value of stand aspect is stored in variable ASPECT in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

Subroutine TRNSLO translates the slope percent entered on the STDINFO keyword record to a ratio value by dividing the slope percent by 100. The translated value of stand slope is stored in variable SLOPE in the PLOT labeled COMMON block.

## Processing event monitor instructions

The event monitor within FVS can be used to conditionally schedule activities, create user-defined output variables, and make the value of keyword record parameter fields the result of a mathematical expression rather than constant values. Certain limits exist that govern the number of events, the amount of memory available to hold expressions, and so on. A PARAMETER statement at the beginning of the OPCOM labeled COMMON block sets these limits. To increase these limits, programmers should modify the OPCOM labeled COMMON block, recompile all the FVS code segments that use the OPCOM labeled COMMON block, and re-link the program executable. Some of these limits can be increased; other limits cannot, without a major rewriting of event monitor computer code. Programmers should pay attention to comment statements giving variable definitions in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block to see which of these limits can be adjusted.

### Processing an IF-THEN-ENDIF expression

Stand management activities can be scheduled by year or cycle. They can also be scheduled contingent upon several factors, which can be called an event. An event is designated in FVS by an IF keyword record followed by a logical expression of some sort that defines the event. Following the logical expression, a THEN keyword record signals the end of the logical expression and the beginning of the activities that will be scheduled only when the event is true. The activities can include one or more FVS keyword records (including those found in extensions) that can be scheduled by year or cycle number. An ENDIF keyword record is entered to signal the end of an event monitor sequence.

#### Subroutines involved and their function

When subroutine INITRE encounters an IF keyword record, it immediately calls subroutine EVIF to begin processing the event monitor sequence. The variable LOPEVN is a logical variable having a value of “.TRUE.” if keyword records being currently entered by the user are part of an event monitor sequence. Subroutine EVIF first checks to see if LOPEVN is “.TRUE.” indicating that another event monitor sequence is already open. If it is, subroutine EVIF calls EVEND, an entry point in subroutine EVTACT, to close the event monitor sequence that is already open so a new sequence may be started.

Subroutine EVIF next checks to make sure adding this new event monitor sequence will not exceed the maximum number allowed in FVS. If the maximum has already been reached, subroutine ERRGRO is called to write an error message to the output file. If room exists in the activity storage arrays, subroutine EVIF calls subroutine EVCOMP to process the logical expression.

Section 7.0 describes how FVS compiles the expressions; section 4.0 discusses the processing sequence FVS uses for evaluating logical expressions during a projection cycle.

When subroutine INITRE encounters a THEN keyword record, it calls EVTHEN, an entry point in subroutine EVTACT. EVTHEN links the internal event number, assigned when the logical expression was compiled, with the specified management activities and stores them for future scheduling. These get stored in array IEVACT(i,j) contained in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block.

When subroutine INITRE encounters an ENDIF keyword record, it calls EVEND, an entry point in subroutine EVTACT. EVEND signals an end to processing the event monitor sequence and increments the internal event number.

#### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine ALGSPP is used to check for valid species codes or species group names.

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine EVKEY is used by subroutine ALGKEY to check for user-defined variables in an expression.

Subroutine EVMKV is used to create a new variable.

Subroutine KEYDMP writes a keyword record to the main output file when the parameter values contain errors severe enough that the keyword record is being rejected.

Subroutine UPCASE is used to convert lower case characters to upper case characters.

### Defining new variables

Allowing users to define their own variables is one powerful feature of the event monitor. Values of these variables will be displayed in the Activity Summary portion of the main output file and can be used in logical expressions or specifications of keyword record parameter settings in a PARMS format. New variables are defined using the COMPUTE keyword record followed by a number of supplemental records defining the new variables. The sequence is closed with an END keyword record.

#### Subroutines involved and their function

When subroutine INITRE encounters a COMPUTE keyword record it calls subroutine EVUSRV to compile and store the expressions defining the variables contained on the supplemental records. Subroutine EVUSRV calls subroutine ALGEXP to read an expression from a supplemental record and utilizes subroutines ALGKEY and EVMKV in a similar fashion as done in processing an IF-THEN-ENDIF sequence. Subroutine EVUSRV then calls subroutine ALGCMP to compile the expression. And since the computation of user-defined variables can be scheduled by year or cycle, subroutine EVUSRV calls subroutine OPNEW to place the action into the activity schedule with an activity code, or option code, 33.

#### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages and sets return status codes.

### Compiling the PARMS notation

With most keyword records that can be scheduled by year or cycle, users have the option of using the PARMS format to specify parameter values. The PARMS format allows users to specify expressions that will be used to calculate parameter values at the time the logical expression becomes true and the management activity is being done. This is a very powerful feature of the event monitor.

#### Subroutines involved and their function

As stated above, when subroutine INITRE encounters a keyword record using the PARMS option it calls subroutine OPNEWC to process it. Subroutine INITRE does not check any of the parameter fields for valid values when the PARMS statement is used (it can’t because their values are not known until the option is retrieved from the activity schedule with OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND).  Subroutine OPNEWC calls subroutine ALGCMP to compile expressions making up the parameter specifications, as described in the IF-THEN-ENDIF specification above. If valid parameters specifications are found, OPNEWC stores the activity in the activity schedule and marks it as “NOT ACCOMPLISHED”.  Parameter specifications will be evaluated at the time the management activity specified by the keyword record is triggered by year, cycle, or condition.

#### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine UPCASE is used to convert lower case characters to upper case characters.

## Reading stand and tree record input data

There are two distinct ways to get stand and tree record input data into FVS. This can be done through ASCII flat files or through database input. A keyword record file is required to run FVS; a tree data file is optional. If stand or tree record input data are coming from a database, the DATABASE keyword record is used in the keyword record file to signal subroutine INITRE that database keyword records follow. Subroutine INITRE transfers control to subroutine DBSIN to process the database keyword records. Subroutine DBSIN calls subroutine DBSOPEN to establish database connections. Other subroutines in the database extension input tree and stand information from the database (see section 3.5.1). Control transfers back to subroutine INITRE when an END keyword record is encountered which signals subroutine DBSIN that it is done processing database keyword records.

Stand level information can be entered on FVS keyword records such as STDINFO and DESIGN.  These are processed as detailed above in section 3.3.1.1. Placement of the DATABASE – END keyword record sequence in the data file is critical. If the DATABASE – END sequence is after keyword records, like STDINFO, that specify stand parameters, parameter values from the database will replace those that were entered by the previous keyword records. The opposite is also true, if the keyword records follow the database sequence, parameter values from the keyword records will replace values that came from the database.

Tree record data, if there is any, may be read from a database or from a flat file, or both. It would be unusual for some of the tree data to be in a database and some of it in a flat file, but it can happen. In fact, several tree data files may be read, in effect, concatenating the individual files. Two additional keyword records signal FVS to input tree record data. These are the TREEDATA and PROCESS keyword records; TREEDATA directly signals FVS to input tree record data from a flat file; PROCESS indirectly signals FVS to input tree record data if none has been read and a NOTREES keyword record was not present in the keyword record file.

If there are there are not enough projectable tree records for a simulation, then one of two things will happen. If the variant includes the full regeneration establishment extension, subroutine INITRE calls ESEZCR, an entry point in subroutine ESINIT, to set flags that will trigger the regeneration establishment model to predict some advanced regeneration to start the simulation. If the variant includes the partial regeneration establishment extension model, entry ESEZCR in subroutine ESINIT is still called and the flags get set but the partial regeneration establishment model does not predict natural regeneration. In this case, the projection will run with no tree records (but they could be added using the PLANT or NATURAL keyword records).

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine INTREE processes tree input data and this may occur at different places in the keyword record processing sequence.

When subroutine INITRE encounters a TREEDATA keyword record, tree data input occurs at that point in the FVS keyword record processing sequence. INITRE immediately calls subroutine INTREE to read the tree record input data.

However, a TREEDATA keyword record is not required in a keyword record set. When subroutine INITRE encounters the PROCESS keyword record it checks to see if the tree record data has been read. If it hasn’t, then subroutine INITRE calls subroutine INTREE to read the tree record input data at this point in the FVS processing sequence. A PROCESS keyword record is required in a keyword record set.

When subroutine INITRE encounters a DATABASE keyword record, signaling that the next set of keyword records pertains to the database extension, it immediately calls subroutine DBSIN. Subroutine DBSIN reads and processes the database extension keyword records. If it encounters a STANDSQL keyword record, subroutine DBSSTANDIN is called to input the stand information; if a TREESQL keyword record is encountered, subroutine DBSTREESIN is called to input tree record data. Both stand and tree data are retrieved with an SQL query. If a TREESQL keyword record is present, subroutine INTREE is called from subroutine DBSIN at this point in the keyword record processing sequence. Subroutine INTREE processes the tree records retrieved from the SELECT SQL statements.

Subroutine INTREE calls subroutine DAMCDS that calls subroutine BASDAM to process damage and severity ratings pertaining to the base model. Subroutine DAMCDS stores insect and disease damage and severity ratings for later processing by subroutine DAMPRO.

Subroutine DAMPRO is called from subroutine INITRE to process damage codes for insect and disease extensions.

Subroutine TRESOR is called from subroutine INITRE to match tree identification numbers with tree index numbers for FVS extensions

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if a user has called for triggering extra write statements to the output file which will be useful in program debugging.

Subroutine ERRGRO contains the various FVS warning and error messages.

Subroutine ESPLT1 is called to store point specific information for the regeneration establishment extension.

Subroutine LNKCHN is called for each tree record to establish it in the sorting sequence.

RDATV and RDTRES are used to see if the western root disease model extension is active and tree list initialization is being used. These two routines will exist as subroutines if the western root disease model extension is part of the variant, or as entry points in subroutine EXRD if the western root disease model extension is not part of the variant.

Subroutine SPCTRN is used to translate unidentified species codes to the closest valid species code in the variant.

Subroutine SPDECD is used to check field 5 of the TREEDATA keyword record for valid species codes when field 5 is used for data screening.

Subroutine UPCASE is used to change lower case species codes to upper case.

## Model calibration and other setup tasks

At this point in the FVS processing sequence the user’s simulation control information and tree data information have been input into FVS. However, subroutine FVS still has many tasks to complete as part of the projection initialization phase. It must initialize any simulation control variables not yet initialized or set by keyword record input, expand the tree data input to a per-acre basis, fill in any missing data values, and calibrate certain model relationships to match the input data.

### Initialization tasks

Subroutine FVS sets up the IY(i) array which specifies cycle boundaries for the entire projection. It then processes and writes option lists for any insect, disease, and economic extensions that are part of the variant and the simulation.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutines OPEXPN, OPCYCL, and OPLIST to process and list the activity schedule. Subroutine OPEXPN expands the activity list so activities specified for all cycles are duplicated once for each cycle. Subroutine OPLIST writes the activity schedule to the main output file.

Subroutine FVS next calls subroutine SETUP to set up the index pointers for species sorting (see discussion of array IND1(k) in section 2.1.5), and subroutine NOTRE to expand the inventory data to a per-acre basis. This is followed by calls to insect and disease code segments, Code segments will exist as subroutines in the appropriate extension if the extension is part of the variant, or as entry points in the appropriate EX__ subroutine if the extension is not part of the variant. If the model is being run with insect and disease extensions, these calls initialize parameters and compute variables needed by those extensions.

The variable ICYC carries the FVS cycle number and is used in various locations throughout the model. ICYC is initialized to 0 after the input and output files are opened. “Cycle 0” is another way of saying “at inventory time”. The variable ICYC is used as an index to the IY(i) array throughout the model, and in a few places (e.g. subroutines DGDRIV and MORTS) to control program logic. For the next tasks, ICYC is set to 1. Certain activities scheduled for cycle 1 (e.g. TREELIST for cycle 1 with field 4 not set to 1) also occur at inventory time.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine OPCSET to set the option pointers for the initialization phase to the ICYC-1 (i.e. cycle 0) options. Subroutine OPCSET sets up the IPCYC(i) array containing activities that need to be done at cycle 0 sorted by ascending activity number.

SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the maximum Stand Density Index for a stand. This will be needed in variants using a Weibull-based crown change model to correctly fill in missing crown ratio values.

### Model calibration and data dubbing

Next is a major task that distinguishes FVS from many other growth models. The primary growth functions for the large and small tree sub-models, and the height-diameter relationships are calibrated to the input data. Calibration of the model to match the input data improves projection results in most cases. However, users may not want this to happen under some conditions and can turn this FVS feature off using the NOCALIB keyword record.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine CRATET, a variant-dependent subroutine, to perform calibration related tasks. Subroutine CRATET also directs writing of the Calibration Statistics section of the main output file and directs the filling in (or “dubbing”) of any data values missing in the input data (e.g. total tree height or crown ratio).

Subroutine CRATET has an extra task in the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). That is to direct: 1) calibration of the ORGANON growth model equations; and 2) dubbing data values missing in the input data using ORGANON equations for valid ORGANON trees. This step is done by calling the ORGANON subroutine PREPARE and does not occur in any of the other FVS variants. Processing then continues as described below. Structural differences of the ORGANON-FVS variants will be further discussed in section 9.0.

#### Calculate site and stand level variables

Some variants use the stands’ mean annual increment as a growth predictor variable; some variants use the species representing the most basal area, also called the “site species” as a growth predictor variable. Subroutine CRATET calls subroutine MBACAL to identify the site species based on plurality of basal area, and subroutine MAICAL to compute mean annual increment. In a bare ground simulation, the call to MBACAL is skipped.

Most growth equations in FVS contain terms for site level variables that have constant values for a stand projection unless climate change modeling is taking place. Examples of these variables include habitat type, site index, slope, aspect, and elevation. In the absence of climate change, these terms only need to be aggregated once with the results stored in vectors that are subscripted by species; these aggregations get used when processing each tree record. Subroutine CRATET calls subroutine RCON to direct the calculation of these terms. In climate change modeling, if any site level variables change, subroutine RCON gets called again from subroutine GRINCR and these aggregations get recomputed. Subroutine GRINCR will be discussed in section 4.0.

Subroutine RCON calls special entry points that are contained in growth modeling subroutines to load site dependent terms. These are: entry DGCONS in subroutine DGF; entry HTCONS in subroutine HTGF; entry REGCON in subroutine REGENT; entry MORCON in subroutine MORTS; and entry CRCONS in subroutine CROWN. All of these subroutines are variant-specific.

Subroutine CRATET then calls subroutine DENSE to compute stand metrics needed during model calibration. FVS is a forward projecting model. Tree input data includes a tree’s current diameter and height, past diameter growth and height growth over some measurement period, and tree mortality. The basic idea in calibrating the growth models is to backdate the stand to its condition 10-years in the past, project the stand forward 10-years using the imbedded growth and mortality functions, compare the projected current stand to the observed current stand, and scale the growth functions so the projected current stand matches the observed current stand.

Subroutine DENSE is called from various places in FVS. A logical variable, LBKDEN, has a value of “.TRUE.” if DENSE needs to backdate the stand for model calibration. Subroutine DENSE backdates the stand if it needs to, and calculates various other values and adjusts them for non-stockable points in the inventory. These other values include average height of the stand, crown competition factor, relative density by species, and point basal area in larger trees, for all tree records.

#### Dead tree records

Subroutine CRATET next deals with the non-projectable tree records (aka mortality). When tree level data is read, subroutine INTREE stores parameters associated with dead tree records in the bottom of the tree data arrays. Trees coded as recent mortality (within the last 5 years) get stored with a tree history code of 7; trees that have been dead for a longer period of time get stored with a tree history code of 9.

Subroutine CRATET identifies the non-projectable tree records. The numbers of records coded as recent mortality, by species, get written to the FVS main output file. Subroutine CRATET then realigns the pointers to the species-ordered sort, eliminating the dead tree indices. (See the discussion of the IND1(i) and ISCT(i,j) arrays in section 2.1.5.)

It is important to note that FVS is not done with the dead tree information yet, and this information is still stored in the bottom of the tree data arrays. Missing information about dead trees still needs to be filled in, dead tree information needs to be passed to the fire and fuels extension, and dead trees in the inventory data get printed in the tree list output file. Dead tree information will get purged from FVS later in the processing sequence by subroutine FVS (see section 3.7).

#### Calibrate height-diameter equation and dub missing heights

Subroutine CRATET then adjusts the height-diameter equation for all species for which there are at least 3 measured heights in the tree data and height-diameter calibration has not been turned off by the user, or by default. Height-diameter equations vary a lot by variant and the appropriate variant overview document should be consulted to increase understanding of this code section. The only height-diameter equations that can be calibrated to the input data are those of the form shown in equation {3.6.2.3.1}. Adjustment of the height-diameter function is done by adjusting the curve’s intercept, B1.

{3.6.2.3.1} HT = 4.5 + exp(B1 + B2 / (DBH + 1.0))

Subroutine CRATET then estimates (dubs) heights for all tree records (live and dead) for which total tree height was missing in the input data. If the damage code indicates the tree has a broken or dead top and these height values are missing, then these values are also estimated.

#### Add dead trees to the snag list

Subroutine CRATET calls FMSSEE to add the dead trees to the FFE snag list. FMSSEE will exist as a subroutine if the fire and fuels extension is part of the variant, or an entry point in subroutine EXFIRE if the fire and fuels extension in not part of the variant.

#### Dub missing crown ratios

Subroutine CRATET next calls subroutine CROWN to control dubbing of any crown ratios missing in the input data (live and dead trees). CROWN calls subroutine DUBSCR for some small sized trees and dead trees. Again this is variant-specific and the appropriate variant overview should be consulted for the equations being used.

#### Calibrate growth equations

In FVS, trees are considered “large” trees for modeling purposes if they are above some threshold diameter that is both variant- and species-specific; otherwise they are considered “small” trees. The FVS large-tree model is diameter growth driven while the small tree model is height growth driven. When periodic increment data is provided as part of the tree record input, FVS attempts to calibrate both of these functions to the input data. The calibration factor, or scale factor, for both of these functions is a multiplier that is a weighted average between the median ratio of observed to predicted values and 1.0. The weight is dependent on how closely the variation in the residuals for the stand being calibrated matches the variation in the residuals for the overall data used to build the model.

If top height, which is the average height of the 40 largest diameter trees, is needed in either of these relationships, subroutine CRATET calls subroutine AVHT40 to compute this value.

Subroutine CRATET calls subroutine DGDRIV to compute initial scale factors for the large-tree diameter growth model. DGDRIV calls subroutine DGF that contains the variant and species dependent growth functions for the individual trees. Starting with the backdated stand condition, diameter growth is predicted for all tree records. However, only trees larger than the threshold diameter are used to calibrate the large-tree diameter growth model.

After subroutine CRATET is done with calibration of the large-tree diameter growth model, it attempts to calibrate the small-tree height growth model. CRATET calls subroutine FINDAG to estimate total tree age for each tree record. This value is used in estimating height growth in some variants and not needed in others. For those variants that do use tree age, this value is computed from site index curves, which are variant- and species-specific, and tree height; for those variants that do not use tree age in the small tree height growth logic, subroutine FINDAG is a “dummy” subroutine that simply returns control to subroutine CRATET without computing tree age. Subroutine REGENT is then called to compute initial scale factors for the small-tree height growth model.

At this point subroutine CRATET is done with the backdated stand, so it calls subroutines PCTILE, DIST, COMP, and DENSE to compute values related to the initial stand inventory which are needed for output. It then counts and prints the number of tree records with dwarf mistletoe.

Stand Density Index (SDI) is used in many variants for estimating mortality and crown ratio change. For variants using SDI, the last task of subroutine CRATET is to call subroutine SDICHK to see if the SDI of the initial stand inventory is above the maximum SDI specified for the site. If it is, then the maximum SDI is reset and a message is printed to the main output file.

This concludes the model calibration portion of the projection initialization phase but there are still a few more things to do before moving on to the projection cycling phase. Subroutine CRATET returns program control to subroutine FVS for further processing.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is called to see if debug write statements need to be executed in a subroutine.

Subroutine MBACAL is called from subroutines CRATET and DENSE to identify the species representing the most basal area in the stand (i.e. the site species).

Subroutine CCFCAL is called from subroutine DENSE to compute crown competition factor. CCFCAL is also called from other places in FVS for this same purpose and to compute crown width for individual tree records.

Subroutine PCTILE is called from subroutine DENSE to compute tree record percentiles in the basal area distribution.

Subroutine PTBAL is called from subroutine DENSE to compute point basal area in larger trees for each tree record.

Subroutine RDPSRT is called from subroutine CRATET to sort tree records by diameter.

Subroutine SPESRT is called by subroutine CRATET to realign pointers in the species-ordered sort of the tree records.

## Final projection initialization tasks

The remaining projection initialization tasks involve computing stand and tree level variables that have not yet been set, initializing variables used in FVS extensions, and writing initial tree and stand conditions to the various output tables.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine ESFLTR in the regeneration establishment extension to collect inventory information for understory and overstory densities and to flag trees in the inventory as “best trees” for the purposes of regeneration establishment.

The control variable, ICYC, is now set back to a value of 0. It will be used to control the projection cycling phase explained in section 4.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine CWIDTH which calls subroutine CWCALC to estimate crown widths for all tree records.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine VOLS to compute volume estimates for the initial inventory. Tree record percentiles in the various volume distributions are then estimated when subroutine FVS calls subroutines PCTILE and DIST for the various volume attributes.

Subroutine FVS then calls subroutine EXTREE to assign example trees to the arrays which will be used in the Attributes of Selected Sample Trees table in the main output file.

If the cover extension is being used, subroutine FVS makes calls to cover extension subroutines to compute shrub densities, browse statistics, and canopy cover estimates for the initial stand inventory.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine STATS to compute and print stand statistics that describe the distribution of stand attributes among sample plots for the input data. Calculation and printing of this information is controlled by the user with the STATS keyword record. The logical variable LSTATS controls these actions in the code and has a default value of “.FALSE.” and a value of “.TRUE.” if the STATS keyword record is used.

Subroutine FVS then needs to write inventory information to various output files. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine DISPLY to write the initial stand statistics to the main output file. Subroutine FVS calls MISPRT to write the dwarf mistletoe infection and mortality information if mistletoe was specified as a damage code in the input data. MISPRT will exist as a subroutine if the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the variant or as an entry point in subroutine EXMIST if the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the variant. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine PRTRLS to write the cycle 0 tree list output if it was called for with the TREELIST keyword record, subroutine FVSSTD to write the cycle 0 information needed by the FVSStand post-processing program if it was called for with the FVSSTAND keyword record, and subroutine NATCRZ to write the cycle 0 information needed by the National Cruise Program if called for with the CRUZFILE keyword record.

At this point FVS is done with the dead trees that were present in the initial inventory. Dead trees are not physically purged (i.e. resetting all the storage locations in the tree data arrays that hold dead tree information back to zeroes); they are purged by resetting the variable IREC2, which is a pointer to the location in the tree data arrays where information for dead tree records starts. Dead tree information is stored at the bottom of the tree data arrays. The maximum number of tree records FVS allows is currently set at 3000 (2000 in the ORGANON-FVS variants) and stored in variable MAXTRE in the PRGPRM labeled COMMON block. So, storage locations 3000-IREC2 to 3000 (2000-IREC2 to 2000 in the ORGANON-FVS variants) contain dead tree information in the bottom of the tree data arrays. Subroutine FVS resets IREC2 to MAXTP1 (also in the PRGPRM labeled COMMON block) which has a value of 3001, or MAXTRE+1, (2001 in ORGANON-FVS variants). In FVS, looping over dead trees goes from IREC2 to MAXTRE, and is preceded by a simple test that if IREC2 is greater than MAXTRE then skip that section of code. So this reassignment of IREC2 effectively frees up those storage locations for later use in storing live tree information.

Subroutine FVS next calls RDMN1 and RDPR to initialize the western root disease model. RDMN1 and RDPR will exist as subroutines if the western root disease extension is part of the FVS executable program, or as entry points in subroutine EXRD if the western root disease extension is not part of the executable program.

Subroutine FVS next calls BRSETP and BRPR to initialize the blister rust model. BRSETP and BRPR will exist as subroutines if the blister rust model is part of the FVS executable program, or as entry points in the EXBR subroutine if the blister rust extension is not part of the executable program.

The final step in projection initialization phase is to set the logical flag, LSTART that is carried in the CONTRL labeled COMMON block, to a value of “.FALSE.” indicating the project initialization phase has been completed. Some subroutines used in projection initialization (e.g. subroutine DGDRIV) have two similar but distinct sections. One part is used in projection initialization and the other is used in projection cycling. These subroutines check the value of variable LSTART to determine which section should be used.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine COMP is used to calculate the species and tree class percentage composition values for various volume categories.

Subroutine DBCHK is called by various subroutines to see if debug output is to be printed.

Subroutine DIST is used to compute diameters corresponding to the nominal percentile points (10, 30, 50, 70, and 90) in the distribution of a stand attribute.

Subroutine ECVOL is used to process volume information for the economics post-processor if an economics analysis is called for.

Subroutine FORTYP is called by subroutine DISPLY to calculate the forest type, size class, and stocking class for printing in the output tables. In the Southern variant (SN), if a user does not specify a maximum stand density index or basal area maximum, then these values are defaulted from the forest type. Consequently, in the SN variant, if forest type changes and user-defined values have not been entered, then the maximum stand density index and basal area maximum are also changed.

Subroutine IAPSRT is called by subroutine ESFLTR to sort trees in the inventory data by plot number.

Subroutine OPFIND is called by subroutine CWIDTH to see if any FIXCW keyword records are scheduled for all cycles.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called by subroutine CWIDTH to process any FIXCW keyword records scheduled for all cycles, and OPDONE, another entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to list the activity as “DONE”.

Subroutine OPGET2 is called by subroutine ESFLTR to check for a TALLYONE option scheduled within 20 years of the inventory year. Subroutine OPGET2 provides an alternative way to retrieve activities where those scheduled for years beyond the current cycle boundaries can be retrieved.

Subroutine PCTILE is used to calculate percentile points in the distribution of annual total cubic foot accretion.

Subroutine VARVOL contains entry points NATCRS, OCFVOL, OBFVOL, and GETEQN. Subroutine VOLS calls entry point NATCRS which calls PROFILE when equations from the National Cruise Program are being used to estimate volumes, or calls other Region specific subroutines (e.g. FORMCL and R6VOL for Region 6; R5HARV for Region 5); VOLS calls entries OCFVOL and OBFVOL or subroutines CFVOL and BFVOL when users change the volume calculation method using field 7 of the VOLUME keyword record. By default, FVS uses the National Cruise Program equations. Entry point GETEQN is used by subroutine NATCRZ to return the volume equation number being used when writing an output file for the National Cruise Program post-processor. Equation numbers used by the National Cruise Program also get written to the FVS main output file. Subroutine VOLS calls subroutines CFTOPK and BFTOPK to compute volume lost to broken or dead tops.

Subroutine VOLKEY is called by VOLS to process any keyword records used to change volume standards or volume equations. These keyword records include MCDEFECT, BFDEFECT, VOLUME, and BFVOLUME.

# Projection Cycling Phase

The projection cycling phase simulates tree growth, mortality, regeneration establishment, and stand management actions as specified by a user in the keyword record file. This phase is the core of the FVS model. Once this phase is completed FVS will be ready to write the specified output tables.

The projection cycling phase is controlled by the variables ICYC and NCYC. ICYC is the current FVS cycle number and NCYC is the number of FVS cycles in a simulation. The default value of NCYC is 1 but it can be set to a value ranging from 2 to 40 using the NUMCYCLE keyword record. The current maximum, 40, can be changed in the PRGPRM code segment (see section 2.1.4).

The FVS control loop and logic can be summed up very simply:

Increment ICYC by 1.

Check the event monitor and simulate harvest, growth, and mortality.

Predict insect and disease effects (if any) and simulate regeneration establishment.

Write end of cycle values to the output files, predict crown ratio change, and update tree records.

Compare ICYC and NCYC; if ICYC is equal to NCYC then the projection cycling phase is completed; if ICYC is less than NCYC then another projection cycle is called for and the process starts over with step 1.

## Processing Sequence Diagrams {-}

### Overall Projection Cycle Sequence {-}

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  PROJECTION CYCLE CONTROL                        │
│                     (FVS Main Loop)                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ ICYC = ICYC + 1  │
                    └──────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ FVS → TREGRO     │
                    └──────────────────┘
                              │
        ┌─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐
        │                                           │
        ▼                                           ▼
┌────────────────┐                         ┌────────────────┐
│  TREGRO calls: │                         │  FVS calls:    │
│                │                         │                │
│  → GRINCR      │                         │  → EXTREE      │
│  → GRADD       │                         │  → DISPLY      │
│                │                         │  → RESAGE      │
│  (Sections     │                         │  → MISPRT      │
│   4.1-4.7)     │                         │  → Extension   │
│                │                         │     outputs    │
│                │                         │  → PRTRLS      │
│                │                         │  → FVSSTD      │
│                │                         │  → NATCRZ      │
│                │                         │  → SYSTEM      │
│                │                         │                │
│                │                         │  (Section 4.8) │
└────────────────┘                         └────────────────┘
        │                                           │
        └─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │  ICYC = NCYC?    │
                    └──────────────────┘
                              │
                ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                │                           │
                ▼                           ▼
        ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐
        │  Yes:        │          │  No:             │
        │  Go to       │          │  Continue to     │
        │  Section 5.0 │          │  next cycle      │
        │  (Summary)   │          │  (increment ICYC)│
        └──────────────┘          └──────────────────┘
```

### TREGRO → GRINCR Detailed Sequence (Sections 4.1-4.2) {-}

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    GRINCR PROCESSING SEQUENCE                    │
│           (Event Monitor, Harvest, Growth, Mortality)            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
    ┌─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┐
    │  Cycle Setup                                       │
    │  ───────────                                       │
    │  • Set FINT (cycle length from IY array)           │
    │  • OPCSET (set option pointers for cycle)          │
    │  • Set LTRIP (record tripling control)             │
    │  • Process SETSITE if scheduled                    │
    │  • Extension setup (root disease, fire, etc.)      │
    └─────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Before-Thinning Event Monitor (IPH=1, IPHASE=1)   │
    │  ────────────────────────────────────────────       │
    │  GRINCR → SILFTY (SILVAH forest type, NE only)     │
    │         → Compute predefined event variables:       │
    │           • SDICAL (SDI maximum)                    │
    │           • SDICLS (current SDI)                    │
    │           • SSTAGE (structural stage)               │
    │         → EVMON ──────────────────────────┐         │
    │                                            │         │
    │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┘        │
    │  │ EVMON Processing:                                │
    │  │ • EVTSTV (load Groups 1,3,4,5 variables)         │
    │  │ • EVAGE (age events if ICYC≥2)                   │
    │  │ • ALGEVL → EVLDX (evaluate expressions)          │
    │  │ • EVPOST → EVALNK (post event if occurred)       │
    │  │                                                   │
    │  │ Actions: compute variables, schedule activities  │
    │  └───────────────────────────────────────┐          │
    │                                            │          │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Thinning and Pruning (Section 4.1.1.2)            │
    │  ───────────────────────────────────────            │
    │  GRINCR → SVOUT (begin-of-cycle visualization)     │
    │         → CUTS ─────────────────────────────┐      │
    │                                              │      │
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
    │  │ CUTS Processing Sequence:                       │
    │  │ ──────────────────────────                      │
    │  │ 1. Setup:                                       │
    │  │    • OPFIND (find thinning requests)            │
    │  │    • Initialize WK4()=0 (trial removals)        │
    │  │    • Set multipliers (SPECPREF, TCONDMLT)       │
    │  │                                                  │
    │  │ 2. Trial Thinning (DO 1400 loop):               │
    │  │    For each scheduled thin:                     │
    │  │      • OPGET (retrieve IACTK, parameters)       │
    │  │      • Process thin type (ICFLAG logic):        │
    │  │        - Diameter limit (BTP/BBA/TPA)           │
    │  │        - From below/above                       │
    │  │        - Proportional                           │
    │  │        - Individual tree                        │
    │  │      • Accumulate WK4() removals                │
    │  │      • Accumulate volumes removed               │
    │  │                                                  │
    │  │ 3. Check Constraints:                           │
    │  │    • Minimum harvest (MINHARV)                  │
    │  │    • Pretend mode (ECON extension)              │
    │  │    • If constraints met → proceed               │
    │  │                                                  │
    │  │ 4. Final Implementation (DO 1700 loop):         │
    │  │    • Apply WK4() removals to PROB()             │
    │  │    • TREDEL (delete zero-TPA records)           │
    │  │    • SPESRT, RDPSRT (resort lists)              │
    │  │                                                  │
    │  │ 5. Output:                                      │
    │  │    • PRTRLS (cut lists, residual lists)         │
    │  │    • FVSSTD, NATCRZ, SVCUTS                     │
    │  │                                                  │
    │  │ 6. Extension interfaces:                        │
    │  │    • FMATV, FMSALV, FMSCUT, FMTREM, FMPRUN      │
    │  │    • GetIsPretendActive, ECHARV                 │
    │  └──────────────────────────────────────────       │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Post-Thinning Updates                              │
    │  ─────────────────────                              │
    │  GRINCR → DENSE (update stand density if thinned)  │
    │         → Compute after-thin event variables:       │
    │           • SDICAL, SDICLS, SILFTY, SSTAGE          │
    │           • Extension calls (CVBROW, CVCNOP, etc.)  │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  After-Thinning Event Monitor (IPH=2, IPHASE=2)    │
    │  ───────────────────────────────────────────        │
    │  GRINCR → EVMON (same logic as before-thin)        │
    │         → EVTSTV (load Groups 2,5 variables)        │
    │         → ALGEVL, EVPOST                            │
    │         → COMCUP → COMPRS (compress tree list)      │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Extension Outbreak Checks                          │
    │  ─────────────────────────                          │
    │  GRINCR → Extension event checks:                   │
    │         → DFTMGO, TMBMAS (Douglas-fir tussock moth) │
    │         → Other insect/disease extensions           │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  GROWTH PREDICTION (Section 4.2)                    │
    │  ───────────────────────────────                    │
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
    │  │ Large-Tree Diameter Growth                 │      │
    │  │ ──────────────────────────                │      │
    │  │ GRINCR → DGDRIV                           │      │
    │  │   → MULTS (retrieve BAIMULT, MANAGED)     │      │
    │  │   → AUTCOR (ARMA(1,1) correlation)        │      │
    │  │   → DGF (predict DG for all trees)        │      │
    │  │      → Store ln(BAI) in WK2()             │      │
    │  │   → Nested loops (species, trees):        │      │
    │  │      • Adjust serial correlation          │      │
    │  │      • Calculate errors                    │      │
    │  │      • DGSCOR (DG error term)             │      │
    │  │      • Add error to DG estimate           │      │
    │  │      • Apply mistletoe multiplier         │      │
    │  │      • Bound to maximum (variant-specific)│      │
    │  │      • Assign to tripled records if LTRIP │      │
    │  │                                            │      │
    │  │ Result: DG() = 10-year increment (inches) │      │
    │  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
    │                      │                              │
    │                      ▼                              │
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
    │  │ Large-Tree Height Growth                   │      │
    │  │ ────────────────────────                  │      │
    │  │ GRINCR → HTGF                             │      │
    │  │   → MULTS (retrieve HTGMULT)              │      │
    │  │   → Nested loops (species, trees):        │      │
    │  │      • Predict HTG                         │      │
    │  │      • For site-index variants:           │      │
    │  │         - FINDAG (estimate age)           │      │
    │  │         - HTCALC (current & future HT)    │      │
    │  │         - HTG = future HT - current HT    │      │
    │  │      • Bound: HT+HTG ≤ morphological max  │      │
    │  │        (TRESZCP keyword)                   │      │
    │  │      • Assign to tripled records if LTRIP │      │
    │  │                                            │      │
    │  │ Result: HTG() = cycle-length (feet)       │      │
    │  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
    │                      │                              │
    │                      ▼                              │
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
    │  │ Small-Tree Growth (REGENT)                 │      │
    │  │ ──────────────────────────                │      │
    │  │ GRINCR → REGENT                           │      │
    │  │   → DBCHK (debug output check)            │      │
    │  │   → MULTS (REGHMULT, REGDMULT)            │      │
    │  │                                            │      │
    │  │ Variants WITHOUT period sub-cycling:      │      │
    │  │   • Calculate mid-cycle CCF, AVH40        │      │
    │  │     (interpolate start/end values)        │      │
    │  │   • Double-nested loops (spp, trees):     │      │
    │  │      - Estimate HTG (10-yr or 5-yr base)  │      │
    │  │      - Weight with large-tree HTG:        │      │
    │  │        XWT = (DBH-Xmin)/(Xmax-Xmin)       │      │
    │  │        HTG_final = (1-XWT)*HTG_small +    │      │
    │  │                    XWT*HTG_large          │      │
    │  │      - Estimate DG from HT-DBH curves     │      │
    │  │      - If DBH < BREAK: use DG_small       │      │
    │  │        else: use DG_large                 │      │
    │  │      - Scale DG to 10-year basis          │      │
    │  │                                            │      │
    │  │ Variants WITH period sub-cycling:         │      │
    │  │   • Divide cycle into ≤5-year periods     │      │
    │  │   • Triple-nested (periods, spp, trees):  │      │
    │  │      - Update stand density each period   │      │
    │  │      - Grow trees incrementally           │      │
    │  │      - WK3(j) = end-of-cycle height       │      │
    │  │   • Calculate final HTG, DG as above      │      │
    │  │                                            │      │
    │  │ Final: assign growth to tripled records  │      │
    │  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
    │                      │                              │
    │                      ▼                              │
    │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
    │  │ Growth Bounds (FIXDG, FIXHTG)              │      │
    │  │ ─────────────────────────────             │      │
    │  │ GRINCR → OPFIND, OPGET, OPDONE            │      │
    │  │   • Check compliance with user bounds     │      │
    │  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  MORTALITY PREDICTION (Section 4.2.1.3)             │
    │  ──────────────────────────────────────             │
    │  GRINCR → MORTS                                     │
    │         → DBCHK                                     │
    │         → OPFIND, OPGET, OPDONE (MORTMULT)          │
    │         → SDICAL (if BAMAX not set)                 │
    │         → Estimate end-of-cycle QMD                 │
    │                                                      │
    │  ┌────── Prognosis-Type Mortality: ────────┐       │
    │  │ • Calculate BA increment                 │       │
    │  │ • Recompute with mortality adjustment:   │       │
    │  │   BA_loss_fraction = BA / BAMAX          │       │
    │  │ • Compute annual approach rate Rb        │       │
    │  │ • Nested loops (species, trees):         │       │
    │  │    - Compute tree mortality rate Ra      │       │
    │  │      (habitat, species, DBH, DG, BA)     │       │
    │  │    - Combine Ra and Rb                   │       │
    │  │    - Apply mortality to PROB()           │       │
    │  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
    │                                                      │
    │  ┌────── SDI-Based Mortality: ──────────────┐       │
    │  │ Iterative process:                        │       │
    │  │ 1. Compute stand trajectory (max SDI)     │       │
    │  │ 2. Estimate mortality level from ΔQMD     │       │
    │  │ 3. Determine if density mortality active: │       │
    │  │    (SDI > 55% of SDI_max by default)      │       │
    │  │ 4. Compute density-related rate RN        │       │
    │  │ 5. Nested loops (species, trees):         │       │
    │  │    • Compute background rate RI           │       │
    │  │    • Apply MORTMULT                       │       │
    │  │    • Use RN if density active, else RI    │       │
    │  │ 6. Call variant-specific redistribution:  │       │
    │  │    → VARMRT, SEAMRT, BMTMRT, NWCMRT,      │       │
    │  │      SCOMRT, TTMRT, UTMRT                 │       │
    │  │ 7. Recompute QMD                          │       │
    │  │ 8. If |ΔQMD| > 0.1": iterate (max 10)     │       │
    │  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
    │                                                      │
    │  Common final steps (all mortality types):          │
    │    → MSBMRT (overmature stand breakup if MORTMSB)   │
    │    → Morphological diameter limit (TREESZCP)        │
    │    → Adjust for BAMAX overshoot (SDI models)        │
    │    → CLMORTS (climate modification)                 │
    │    → OPFIND, OPGET, OPDONE (FIXMORT)                │
    │                                                      │
    │  Result: PROB() reduced, OMORT() set                │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ Return to TREGRO │
                    │ Call GRADD       │
                    └──────────────────┘
```

Step 1 happens in subroutine FVS. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine TREGRO which calls subroutine GRINCR to handle step 2 and subroutine GRADD to handle step 3. Both GRINCR and GRADD call several other subroutines, as outlined in the following sections. Subroutine FVS then calls several subroutines to handle step 4, and performs step 5. Steps 2-4 will be explained in detail in the following sections.

## Event monitor and harvest

Checking the event monitor and simulating harvest both occur at the beginning of a projection cycle in FVS. Subroutine FVS calls subroutine TREGRO which calls subroutine GRINCR to control these tasks.

### Subroutines involved and their function

There are some model control tasks that subroutine GRINCR needs to accomplish at the start of each projection cycle.
