First the cycle length, FINT, is set; next subroutine OPCSET is called to set up the option pointers for the cycle; the logical variable LTRIP is set to control whether record tripling will happen during the cycle; subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND) are called to process any SETSITE keyword records scheduled for the cycle; if a SETSITE keyword record is present, subroutine HABTYP gets called to decode the habitat type, if habitat type is being reset as part of the SETSITE options, and subroutine RCON gets called to recalculate growth equation species-level constants; and various subroutines get called to set up variables needed by FVS extensions (e.g. root disease, fire and fuel effects, and others).

Thinning to a relative density target, as done in the SILVAH (Marquis and Ernst 1992) growth model, is a management option in the Northeast (NE) variant. Subroutine GRINCR calls SILFTY, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, to compute the SILVAH forest type before thinning. For the NE variant, possible values for the SILVAH forest type range from 0 to 5; in all other variants, the SILVAH forest type will be 0.

The event monitor is an integral part of all FVS variants and its’ capabilities are discussed in section 5.5 of the EFVS Guide. A detailed discussion of event monitor structure is presented in section 7.0 of this document. Subroutine GRINCR next directs the computation of some predefined before-thinning event monitor variables. Subroutine SDICAL is called to compute the before-thinning stand SDI maximum; SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the current stand SDI by two methods (Reineke 1933 and Zeide 1983); and subroutine SSTAGE is called to compute the before-thinning stand structural stage.

Subroutine GRINCR then calls subroutine EVMON to see if any before-thinning actions need to be scheduled. The variable IPH is a local variable in both subroutines GRINCR and EVMON that indicates the event monitor phase number. The value for this variable is passed from subroutine GRINCR to subroutine EVMON through the EVMON argument list. This variable is used in subroutine EVMON to set the event monitor phase number, variable IPHASE that is carried in the OPCOM labeled COMMON block. The phase number is an important variable in controlling event monitor logic. The variable IPH, and consequently variable IPHASE, have a value of 1 if the event monitor is being called before thinning and 2 if the event monitor is being called after thinning.

#### Checking the event monitor for before-thinning actions

Before-thinning actions include computing predefined and custom output variables based on stand conditions before harvesting occurs, or evaluating expressions that conditionally schedule management activities, such as a thinning, based on before-thinning stand conditions.

Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVTSTV to load values of predefined event monitor variables in Groups 1, 3, 4, and 5 (see EFVS Table 5-2 for a list of variables in Groups 1, 3, and 4; Group 5 variables are user-defined).

If the cycle number, ICYC, is 2 or greater, subroutine EVAGE is called to age an event that has already occurred and resets it as viable for occurring at some other time.

Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine ALGEVL to evaluate expressions. Expressions may be used in computing user-defined variables or in keyword record parameter fields using the PARMS format. Subroutine ALGEVL calls subroutine EVLDX to load values of saved variables or results of functions like SPMCDBH into storage registers for further computing.

Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVPOST to post the year the event occurred. This means changing the second value in the row of the IVENTS(i,j) array (i.e. j = 2, i = the row holding information for this event). This storage location stores the year the activity occurred, if it occurs, or -1 if it does not occur. EVPOST calls subroutine EVALNK to determine if the event is linked to an activity group.

This concludes the event monitor check before thinning and control returns to subroutine GRINCR for further processing.

#### Processing thinning and pruning requests

If the cycle number is greater than or equal to 2, subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine SVOUT to write the beginning-of-cycle output file for the stand visualization post-processor.

Subroutine GRINCR then calls subroutine CUTS to process all pruning and thinning management activities. It is important to note that harvesting occurs at the beginning of a projection cycle. So harvests scheduled at any time during the projection cycle are actually done at the beginning of that projection cycle. If harvesting at a particular year is important to a user, then manipulation of the cycle boundaries using the TIMEINT or CYCLEAT keyword records will be necessary.

Subroutine CUTS is simple in concept, but very complicated in terms of coding; it makes heavy use of logical variables and work arrays. Fortunately, the subroutine is well documented with comment statements. CUTS is responsible for processing minimum harvest constraints (MINHARV keyword record), setting multipliers for use in the harvest priority algorithm (SPECPREF and TCONDMLT keyword records), accounting for portions of a harvest that may be left in the woods (YARDLOSS keyword record), removing portions of a trees’ crown ratio (PRUNE keyword record), and processing all harvest requests scheduled for the cycle (THIN___ and SETPTHIN keyword records).

Subroutine CUTS interfaces with the fire and fuels extension by calling: FMATV to see if the fire extension is active; FMSALV to process harvesting of dead trees with the SALVAGE keyword record; FMSCUT to update the snag list; FMTREM to save removals for processing with the TREEBIO event monitor function; and FMPRUN to update debris pools with pruning slash. FMATV, FMSALV, FMSCUT, FMTREM, and FMPRUN will exist as subroutines if the fire and fuels extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXFIRE if the fire and fuels extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutine CUTS also interfaces with the Economic extension. GetIsPretendActive, an entry point in subroutine ECSTATUS, is called to see if the PRETEND keyword record has been specified. The pretend mode allows users to get an economic analysis of a proposed thinning without actually performing the thinning in FVS. ECHARV is called to accumulate board foot volume removal information. ECHARV will exist as a subroutine if the economics extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXECON if the economics extension is not part of the program executable.

There is an older economics post-processing program called CHEAPOII. Subroutine CUTS calls subroutines ECREMS and ECOUT to produce the necessary information to interface with this program. CHEAPOII has been completely replaced by the ECON extension and is no longer used; code related to the CHEAPOII program should be deleted from the FVS system.

4.1.1.2.1 How subroutine CUTS works

The harvest concept in subroutine CUTS is to loop over all thinning requests, accumulate the harvest information, and reduce the trees per acre representation for each tree record affected by a thinning. This is done on a “trial basis” first and the accumulated harvest is compared to the minimum harvest constraint. If the minimum harvest constraint is not met, or these thinnings are part of the pretend mode for an economic analysis, then the thinning requests are not finalized. Otherwise, a final pass is made over all tree records and results from the trial thinnings are fully implemented.

Subroutine CUTS calls subroutine OPFIND to see if any thinning requests are scheduled for the current cycle. The trial thinning vector, WK4(i), which accumulates the removed trees per acre values for tree “i” as thinning requests are processed, is initialized to zero along with other control variables like those used to accumulate removed volumes. The DO 1400 loop processes all thinning requests, one at a time, and accumulates the trial thinning values. For each thinning request scheduled for the current cycle, OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND,  is called to retrieve parameters associated with the thinning request along with the activity number, IACTK, which identifies the type of thinning that is being processed. The IACTK value, or a transformation of it stored in variable ICFLAG, is used within the DO 1400 loop to control the logic needed to process the thinning request.

The DO 1700 loop implements results from the trial thinnings if minimum harvest constraints are met and the cutting subroutine in not in the pretend mode for an economic analysis.

If the trees per acre representation for a tree record is reduced to zero (i.e. all of the trees represented by that tree record are cut), subroutine CUTS calls subroutine TREDEL to delete those tree records from the tree list. Subroutine SPESRT is then called to realign the species ordered sort for the remaining tree records and subroutine RDPSRT is called to sort the IND(i) array from largest to smallest, in terms of diameter, for residual trees in the stand.

Subroutine CUTS calls several subroutines to produce tree lists for cut tree records and the residual stand. Subroutine PRTRLS produces a cut tree list, requested with the CUTLIST keyword record, and an after treatment live tree list; subroutine FVSSTD is called to write a cut tree list for the FVSStand post-processer, requested with the FVSSTAND keyword record; subroutine NATCRZ is called to write a cut tree list for the National Cruise Program post-processor; and subroutine SVCUTS is called to write files needed for a stand visualization of the thinning if requested using the SVS keyword record.

Processing control returns to subroutine GRINCR to do some post-thinning updating of stand statistics and other control variables. GRINCR calls subroutine DENSE to update stand density statistics if any thinning occurred. GRINCR next computes values of some predefined after-thinning event monitor variables. Subroutine SDICAL is called to compute the after-thinning stand SDI maximum; SDICLS, which is an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the after-thinning stand SDI by two methods (Reineke 1933 and Zeide 1983); SILFTY, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is called to compute the after-thinning SILVAH forest type; and subroutine SSTAGE is called to compute the after-thinning stand structural stage. Other code segments are called for extensions that may be part of the model (e.g. CVBROW and CVCNOP for the cover extension). These will be individual subroutines if the extension is part of the model, or entry points in the corresponding “EX__” subroutine if the extension is not part of the model (e.g. subroutine EXCOV for the cover extension). GRINCR is now ready to call the event monitor for processing after-thinning actions.

#### Checking the event monitor for after-thinning actions

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine EVMON, with the event monitor phase number set to 2, to see if any after-thinning actions need to be scheduled. After-thinning actions include computing predefined and custom output variables based on stand conditions after harvesting occurs or evaluating expressions that conditionally schedule management activities based on post-thinning conditions.

The logic is basically the same as discussed in section 4.1.1.1. Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVTSTV to load values of predefined event monitor variables in Groups 2 and 5 (see EFVS Table 5-2 for variables in 2; Group 5 variables are user-defined). Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine ALGEVL to evaluate expressions. Subroutine ALGEVL calls subroutine EVLDX to load values of saved variables or results of functions like SPMCDBH into storage registers for further computing. Subroutine EVMON calls subroutine EVPOST to post the year the event occurred and control returns to subroutine GRINCR.

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine COMCUP which interfaces with subroutine COMPRS to compress the tree list. This may be necessary when entire tree records are removed as part of the thinning process.

Next, subroutine GRINCR calls various code segments pertaining to insect and disease extensions (e.g. DFTMGO and TMBMAS for the Douglas-fir Tussock Moth extension). These code segments will be individual subroutines if the extension is part of the model, or entry points in the corresponding “EX__” subroutine if the extension is not part of the model (e.g. EXDFTM for the Douglas-fir Tussock Moth extension). These subroutines are used to determine if events like a tussock moth outbreak will occur in this projection cycle.

Subroutine GRINCR is now ready to predict tree growth and mortality for the current projection cycle.

### Auxiliary subroutines

AUTSTK, an entry point in subroutine CUTSTK, is used to compute a value for normal full stocking for the automatic thinning option (THINAUTO keyword record).

CCCLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of canopy cover for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

CLSSTK, an entry point in subroutine CUTSTK, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of trees per acre or basal area for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

Subroutine COMP is used to determine species by tree class composition statistics for removed trees, removed volumes, and residual trees.

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine DIST is used to compute diameters corresponding to the nominal percentile points (10, 30, 50, 70, and 90) in the distribution of removed trees and removed volumes.

Subroutine ESTUMP is used to add stumps to the stump list for processing of regeneration sprouting at the end of the projection cycle.

Subroutine ERRGRO is used to post warning and error messages to the FVS output file.

Subroutine LNKCHN is used by subroutine SPESRT to establish the IND2(i) values for residual trees when entire tree records are removed and subsequently deleted by thinning requests.

MISCPF is used to process the mistletoe cutting preference (MISTPREF keyword record) and MISGET is used to retrieve the mistletoe rating for the current tree record. MISCPF and MISGET will exist as subroutines if the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXMIST if the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the program executable.

OPCHPR, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to change the value of the stored parameter associated with the CUTEFF keyword record.

OPDEL1, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to mark a thinning request as “DELETED OR CANCELLED” if the thinning request cannot be processed for some reason.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to set the year a thinning option is actually accomplished.

Subroutine PCTILE is used to compute the percentile points in the distribution of removed trees and removed volumes.

RDCLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of relative density (Curtis 1982) for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

RDCLS2, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of relative density (Marquis and Ernst 1992) for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

RDSLTR, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute the relative density (Marquis and Ernst 1992) contribution of a given tree record.

SDICLS, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute a stocking value in terms of stand density index for a specified group of tree records defined by a diameter and/or height range.

Subroutine SETUP is called by subroutine SPESRT to establish the IND1(i) and ISCT(i,j) values for residual trees when entire tree records are removed and subsequently deleted by thinning requests.

SILFTY, an entry point in subroutine SDICAL, is used to compute the forest type according to the SILVAH (Marquis and Ernst 1992) definitions.

Subroutine SVOUT is used to produce a file for post-treatment stand visualization when a salvage removal is called for by the fire and fuels extension and no live trees were removed.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in section 8.0. They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Growth and Mortality

Trees are considered “large” trees for FVS modeling purposes when they are larger than some species and variant dependent threshold diameter. These threshold diameters and detailed descriptions of equations used to grow large trees and small trees can be found in the variant overview documents. A general description of the FVS large and small tree models as they are used in model calibration can be found in section 7.2 of the EFVS Guide.

FVS mortality models are one of three types: 1) the Prognosis mortality model; 2) the SDI based mortality model; or 3) the ORGANON mortality model. A fourth type, the TWIGS based mortality model, has now been replaced with SDI based mortality models in the Lake States (LS), Central States (CS), and Northeast (NE) variants. A general description of the Prognosis, SDI, and TWIGS mortality models can be found in section 7.3 of the EFVS Guide. A description of the ORGANON mortality model can be found in the overview documents for the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). Structural differences of the ORGANON-FVS variants will be further discussed in section 9.0.

### Subroutines involved and their function

The order in which FVS simulates stand-changing events is important. FVS is a forward predicting model. That is to say, it predicts future stand conditions from current stand conditions. Harvesting occurs at the beginning of a growth projection cycle prior to growth prediction. So pruning and harvesting affects growth rates through modified crown ratio and stand density attributes.

Intuitively, if you look at the model flow diagram (figure 2-1), mortality seems to work the other way around; mortality is predicted after growth so it appears that mortality is being predicted at the end of a projection cycle. However, this isn’t really the case. FVS is still in a forward predicting mode and estimating the mortality that will occur during the projection cycle, but taking into consideration competition due to individual tree growth that will occur during the cycle.

The processing sequence through this section of code is to obtain an estimate of:

large tree diameter growth

large tree height growth

small tree height growth

small tree diameter growth

mortality

This is subtly different than the language used in Figure 2-1. Figure 2-1 presents the general processing sequence in conceptual terms; the language here reflects the actual programming sequence. For example, in Figure 2-1 we say “grow large trees (in order: diameter, height)” but here we say “obtain an estimate of: 1) large tree diameter growth, 2) large tree height growth”. Diameter and height growth is estimated for all trees (large and small) using equations in the large-tree portion of FVS; height and diameter growth is estimated for only a portion of the trees using equations in the small-tree portion of FVS; and estimates are combined or discarded as appropriate for the variant and species.

Notice that a trees’ crown ratio change, due to tree growth and changes in stand density, is yet to be predicted. This occurs at the very end of a growth projection cycle and will be discussed in section 4.5.

#### Growing the large trees

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine DGDRIV to calculate a large-tree diameter growth estimate for all tree records. DGDRIV is one of those subroutines containing two sections; the top section is used for growth estimation in projection cycling; the bottom section is used for calibration in projection initialization.

Subroutine DGDRIV retrieves any multipliers or management flags scheduled for the current projection cycle with calls to subroutine MULTS.

Large tree diameter growth (or the logarithm of basal area increment in most variants) is estimated using a regression equation with independent variables being individual tree attributes and current stand conditions. An error term is added to the estimate. Error terms are correlated from cycle-to-cycle so the relative magnitude of an individual trees’ estimate is correlated from one projection cycle to the next. In effect, a tree growing well one cycle is likely to grow well the next cycle, and a tree growing poorly is likely to continue growing poorly, to some extent. Periodic increment in large tree diameter growth is considered as an autoregressive moving average time series model (ARMA(1,1)). DGDRIV calls subroutine AUTCOR to compute the variance and covariance multipliers for the current projection cycle.

Subroutine DGDRIV calls subroutine DGF to obtain large tree diameter growth estimates for all the tree records. Subroutine DGF contains regression equations for each species. It is structured as nested DO loops with the outside loop controlling species and the inside loop controlling tree records within species. The argument list for subroutine DGF consists of the array of tree diameters to be used. So in the calibration phase of projection initialization subroutine DGF is called with the array of backdated diameters, and in the growth estimation phase of projection cycling it is called with the tree diameters at the beginning of the projection cycle. Subroutine DGF stores estimated diameter growth for each tree record in terms of natural logarithm of basal area increment in work array WK2(i).

Subroutine DGDRIV has an extra task in the two ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). That is to direct estimation of large tree diameter and height growth, crown ratio change, and mortality using ORGANON equations for valid ORGANON trees. This step is done by calling the ORGANON subroutine EXECUTE and does not occur in any of the other FVS variants. Processing then continues somewhat as described below, with structural differences as discussed in section 9.0.

Subroutine DGDRIV then enters its own nested species and trees-within-species DO loops. For each species, the serial correlation of diameter growth estimates from one cycle to the next is adjusted for the cycle length and diameter growth errors are calculated. The scale factors are attenuated and then the tree loop within species is entered. For each tree record, diameter growth is converted from ln(DDS) terms to inches. DGDRIV calls subroutine DGSCOR to calculate the diameter growth error term and then adds the error to the diameter growth estimate. The diameter growth estimate is multiplied by a factor to account for the negative impacts of dwarf-mistletoe, if any, on diameter growth. Diameter growth is then bounded to a maximum value (diameter growth is only constrained in some variants). Diameter growth is similarly assigned to tree record triples if record tripling is in effect and control returns to subroutine GRINCR. Diameter growth estimates after subroutine DGDRIV are on a 10-year basis. These will be scaled to the cycle length at the end of the growth projection cycle in subroutine GRADD.

Subroutine HTGF has a similar construction as subroutine DGF does. It has nested species and trees-within-species DO loops controlling subroutine execution. Subroutine MULTS is called to retrieve large-tree height growth multipliers. Each trees’ height growth is bounded so current height plus height growth does not exceed a morphological maximum height for the species as entered with the TRESZCP keyword record. Height growth estimates are assigned to record triples if record tripling is in effect and control returns to subroutine GRINCR. Height growth estimates at the end of subroutine HTGF are on a cycle-length basis.

For variants using site index curves to estimate height growth, two other subroutines play a major role in large tree height growth estimation. Subroutine HTCALC contains equations for the site index curves being used for each species. Subroutine HTGF calls subroutine FINDAG to estimate a trees’ age based on a trees’ height and species using the equations in subroutine HTCALC. Subroutine HTGF then adds 10 years to this age and calls HTCALC to obtain an estimate of tree height at the end of the projection cycle based on tree age and species. Potential height growth is then the difference between the estimated beginning- and end-of cycle heights.

#### Growing the small trees

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine REGENT to estimate height and diameter growth using equations for trees smaller than a threshold diameter. Upon completion of subroutine REGENT, all trees will have an estimate of height and diameter growth. Whether that estimate is the estimate using the large tree equations in subroutines DGF and HTGF or the small tree equations contained in subroutine REGENT, or a weighted average of the two, depends on the attribute being estimated, the diameter of the tree, and one or more threshold diameter.

4.2.1.2.1 Threshold diameters

Several threshold diameters are used in subroutine REGENT:

For height growth, two threshold diameters are used. These are contained in local arrays subscripted by species, usually called XMIN(i) and XMAX(i). For species i, an estimate of height growth using small tree equations contained in subroutine REGENT is only calculated for trees with diameter (DBH(i)) less than XMAX(i). Height growth estimates from the small-tree model are weighted with the height growth estimates from the large tree model over a range of diameters, XMIN(i) to XMAX(i), in order to smooth the transition between estimates from the two models. In other words, the closer a tree’s DBH(i) value is to the minimum diameter XMIN(i), the more the growth estimate will be weighted towards the small-tree growth model. The closer a tree’s DBH(i) value is to the maximum diameter XMAX(i), the more the growth estimate will be weighted towards the large-tree growth model. If a tree’s DBH(i) value falls outside of the range given by XMIN(i) and XMAX(i), then the model will use only the estimates from the small-tree equations or large-tree equations in the growth estimate. The weight applied to the growth estimate is calculated using equation {4.2.1.2.1}, and applied as shown in equation {4.2.1.2.2}. The range of diameters for each species is shown in the appropriate variant overview document.

{4.2.1.2.1}XWT = 0DBH(i) < Xmin

XWT = (DBH(i) - Xmin) / (Xmax - Xmin)Xmin < DBH(i) < Xmax

XWT = 1DBH(i) > Xmax

{4.2.1.2.2}Estimated growth = [(1 - XWT) * STGE] + [XWT * LTGE]

where:

iis the FVS tree index

XWT is the weight applied to the growth estimates

DBH(i) is tree diameter at breast height

Xmax is the maximum DBH, XMAX(i), in the diameter range

Xmin is the minimum DBH, XMIN(i), in the diameter range

STGE is the height growth estimate obtained using the small-tree equations

LTGE is the height growth estimate obtained using the large-tree equations

For diameter growth, weighting of the estimate obtained using the large tree equations with that obtained using the small tree equations does not occur; one or the other is used. The one used depends on a different threshold diameter, also specified in the variant overview document. The threshold diameter used in deciding which estimate to use for diameter growth may be contained locally in subroutine REGENT, or it may be contained in an array subscripted by species called BREAK(i) in the GGCOM labeled COMMON block and initialized in subroutine BLKDAT. For species i, trees with DBH(i) less than the threshold diameter are assigned the diameter growth estimate obtained using the small tree diameter growth equations; trees with DBH(i) greater than or equal to the threshold diameter are assigned the diameter growth estimate obtained using the large tree diameter growth equations.

For a few species in some variants, equations contained in subroutine REGENT are used to estimate height and diameter growth for all sized trees. For example, this happens with pinyon pine in the Central Rockies (CR) variant. In these cases, the logic is the same as just discussed with the threshold diameters being set to artificially high values so only estimates using the small tree equations are used.

4.2.1.2.2 Growth estimation and calibration

Subroutine REGENT is another one of those subroutines containing two sections; the top section is used for growth estimation in projection cycling; the bottom section is used for calibration in projection initialization. The structure of each section is similar, and understanding the top section will lead to understanding the bottom section. First, the overall structure of subroutine REGENT will be described and then this structure will be broken down into more detail.

For most variants, a single pair of nested species and trees-within-species DO loops control subroutine execution. In these variants, height growth is estimated for the period length for which the small tree equations were fit (10-years, except for the Klamath Mountain variant (NC) which is 5-years), scaled to the cycle length, and then weighted with height growth estimates previously calculated using the large tree equations. Diameter growth is then estimated for the cycle length and scaled to a 10-year basis. Diameter growth gets scaled back to a cycle length basis in subroutine UPDATE when stand statistics are updated at the end of the projection cycle (see section 4.6).

Some variants use a slightly different logic because the small tree height growth equations were fit to 5-year data. To avoid bias associated with projection cycles longer than the period to which the equation was fit, the projection cycle is first divided into periods that are no longer than 5-years in length (i.e. a 10-year projection cycle would have 2 periods of 5-years; a 7-year projection cycle would have 2 periods with the first being 5-years and the second being 2-years; a 13-year projection cycle would have 3 periods with the first two being 5-years and the third being 3 years, etc.). A triple-nested DO loop structure is used to estimate end of cycle tree height for each tree record which gets stored in work array WK3(j), where j is the tree index. The outside loop is over periods, the middle loop is over species, and the inner loop is over tree records within species. Stand density statistics and tree attributes are updated each period. The height estimate for the last period is scaled to the length of the last period. Double nested species and trees-within-species DO loops are then entered. Height growth for the projection cycle is obtained by subtracting the start-of-cycle tree height from the end-of-cycle tree height. This estimate gets weighted with height growth estimates previously calculated using the large tree equations as discussed above. Diameter growth is estimated and then scaled to a 10-year basis for rescaling in subroutine UPDATE.

4.2.1.2.2.1 A closer look at the logic

The overall structure will now be broken down into more detail. Small tree height growth is estimated using regression equations with independent variables being individual tree attributes and current stand conditions. Once small tree height growth is obtained, small tree diameter growth is estimated using species-specific height-diameter curves. Default height-diameter curves by species for a variant are detailed in the variant overview document but the default coefficients will have been changed if they were calibrated to the input data as described in section 3.6.1.

Subroutine REGENT first calls subroutine DBCHK to see if debug output is to be written.

For variants using sub-cycling over periods, the number of periods and length of each period are computed and necessary independent variables containing the beginning-of-cycle values are initialized.

Subroutine REGENT then retrieves any multipliers or management flags scheduled for the current projection cycle with calls to subroutine MULTS.

Mid-cycle measures of stand density are needed by subroutine REGENT in all variants. Trees coming out of the regeneration establishment model (see section 4.4) use equations in subroutine REGENT to grow trees in height from the time they are age 5 to the end of the projection cycle in which they become established. So estimates of stand density are needed 5 years into a projection cycle. Also, in variants using period sub-cycling, estimates of stand density are needed at the beginning of each period. The methods by which estimates of stand density are computed are completely different depending on whether period sub-cycling is being used.

For variants that do not use period sub-cycling, mid-period crown competition factor and average height of the 40 largest diameter trees is calculated by interpolation of these values at the start and end of the projection cycle. Remember that values of these variables are needed to estimate growth on trees in the regeneration establishment model which is being called near the end of the projection cycle, after growth has been estimated on all trees previously in the inventory. So values of these variables for the end of the projection cycle, prior to regeneration establishment, can be calculated.

For variants using period sub-cycling, the process is much more complicated since estimates of stand crown competition factor and basal area are needed for the start of each period for normal processing. Note that if the projection cycle is more than 5 years in length, then start of period estimates can be used for calculating the values needed for estimating growth on regeneration establishment trees; if the projection cycle length is less than 5 years in length then all growth on regeneration establishment trees will be estimated in the regeneration establishment subroutines. The contribution of large trees to stand basal area and crown competition factor is computed from 10-year predicted diameter increment. This value is annualized and then multiplied by the period sub-cycle length to determine the contribution of each tree for the sub-cycle. A 1% annual rate of mortality is assumed in this calculation. The contribution of small trees is based on growth predictions made for the preceding period sub-cycle. Subroutine CCFCAL is called to estimate the crown competition factor for each tree record in this calculation. If necessary, the height-diameter function used in diameter growth estimation is then adjusted based on stand crown competition factor and average height of the 40 largest diameter trees; this is only needed in some variants using sub-cycling logic.

In variants using period sub-cycling, the triple nested DO loops to estimate tree height at the end of the projection cycle is next. Subroutine CCFCAL is called at several places in the looping structure to estimate the crown competition factor for individual trees for the period sub-cycle.

In all variants, the double nested DO loop structure to estimate diameter and height growth is next. These loops follow the general structure discussed above. Height and diameter growth are then assigned to tripled tree records if record tripling is in effect and program control returns to subroutine GRINCR.

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine OPFIND to check for any FIXDG or FIXHTG keyword records scheduled for the projection cycle. If any are found, OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to retrieve parameters associated with each of these keyword records and height and diameter growth estimates for all tree records are checked for compliance with these parameters. OPDONE, another entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called to mark the activities’ disposition.

FVS is now done with basic growth estimates. However, growth estimates may be modified later in the projection cycle to account for fertilization or insect and disease effects on growth.

#### Mortality

Mortality is estimated using either the Prognosis-type mortality model or SDI-based mortality model in all variants except the ORGANON-FVS variants (OC and OP). Both of these mortality model types are described in the EFVS guide and a detailed discussion of the equations used for a particular variant can be found in the variant overview document.

In the two ORGANON-FVS variants, mortality for all tree records will be estimated using the ORGANON mortality equations or the SDI-based mortality model depending on whether there are valid ORGANON trees in the input data or not. The ORGANON mortality model is described in the OC and OP variant overview documents. Structural differences in the two ORGANON-FVS variants are discussed in more detail in section 9.0.

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine MORTS to estimate mortality. Subroutine MORTS may call another subroutine which distributes mortality using variant-specific methods (subroutine VARMRT for the CA, CR, CS, EC, LS, NE, and SN variants; subroutine SEAMRT for the AK variant; subroutine BMTMRT for the BM variant; subroutine NWCMRT for the NC variant; subroutine SCOMRT for the SO variant; subroutine TTMRT for the TT variant; subroutine UTMRT for the UT variant). Mortality subroutines estimate the number of trees to kill and distribute that mortality across tree records by reducing the trees per acre representation, PROB(j), for each tree record j.

Subroutine MORTS calls subroutine DBCHK to see if debug output is called for and then calls subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND) to process any mortality multipliers scheduled for the projection cycle.

Maximum basal area and maximum stand density index are two measures of the maximum capacity of an area to grow trees. Maximum basal area can be entered directly using the BAMAX keyword record. Individual species’ stand density index maximums can be entered using the SDIMAX keyword record. Maximum stand density index for a stand is a weighted average of the individual species’ stand density index maximums, weighted by the proportion of basal area for a species to the total stand basal area. If a basal area maximum has not been entered, subroutine MORTS calls subroutine SDICAL to assign a basal area maximum that corresponds to the maximum stand density index for the stand. This step is needed by the climate change extension.

Subroutine MORTS estimates the quadratic mean diameter (QMD) at the end of the projection cycle. It is at this point that the two types of FVS mortality models begin to diverge in terms of logic.

4.2.1.3.1 Prognosis-type mortality model

In variants that use the Prognosis-type mortality model, the change in basal area increment is computed from diameter growth that was estimated previously in the projection cycle. This estimate of basal area increment does not account for mortality. So basal area increment is recalculated by taking the basal area at the beginning of the cycle and projecting it forward 10 years, assuming that a proportion of the predicted basal area increment will be lost to mortality. This proportion is the stand basal area divided by the basal area maximum for the stand. So when stand basal area is equal to the maximum stand basal area, all of the predicted basal area increment will be absorbed by mortality. The mortality rate calculated in this manner is converted to an annual estimate and later used to calculate the annual approach to maximum basal area mortality rate, Rb, discussed in the EFVS guide.

A mortality rate for each individual tree record is then computed based on habitat type (or plant association), species, tree diameter, diameter increment, estimated potential diameter increment, stand basal area, and relative diameter. This annual mortality rate is called Ra in the EFVS guide.

The two mortality rates are then combined are then combined as discussed in the EFVS guide.

4.2.1.3.2 SDI-based mortality model

For variants using the SDI-based mortality model, mortality is implemented in two steps; first the number of mortality trees is estimated based on the change in QMD during the projection cycle and SDI relationships, and then mortality gets distributed to individual tree records. Since estimated change in QMD is a function of which trees get killed, this is an iterative procedure.

Two types of mortality are estimated: (1) background mortality which accounts for occasional mortality not attributable to stand density (i.e. competition), and (2) density related mortality which is a function of stand density, tree vigor, a trees’ social position and shade tolerance, and other factors. A detailed discussion of the logic used in the SDI-based mortality model is presented in section 7.3.2 of the EFVS guide.

Subroutine MORTS computes the stand trajectory using equations for maximum SDI. Using the estimated change in QMD, the number of mortality trees is estimated. A determination is made whether density related mortality is in effect using the relationship between current stand SDI and the lower threshold of the maximum SDI (default 55% of maximum SDI). A density related mortality rate, RN, is computed which is a rate when applied to each tree record would meet the desired mortality level.

4.2.1.3.3 Both mortality models

A double nested species and trees-within-species DO loop structure is entered. A background mortality rate, RI, is calculated for each tree record. Mortality multipliers entered with the MORTMULT keyword record are applied to the background mortality rate. The mortality rate applied to each tree record is the background rate, RI, if density related mortality is not in effect, or the density related rate, RN, if density related mortality is in effect.

For SDI-based mortality models, subroutine MORTS then calls one of the subroutines listed above to redistribute mortality to individual tree records according to variant-specific equations. A new QMD is calculated based on this estimate of mortality. If the difference between the initial estimate of QMD and this new estimate of QMD is greater than 0.1”, mortality is recalculated based on the new estimate of QMD. The iteration terminates when the difference in QMD values is less than or equal to 0.1” or a maximum number of iterations has been reached (currently set at 10).

For SDI-based mortality, the breakup of an over mature stand can be simulated using parameters entered with the MORTMSB keyword record. Subroutine MORTS checks to see if this is in effect. If so, it computes the additional mortality in trees per acre that needs to be accounted for and calls subroutine MSBMRT to distribute the additional mortality across the tree records as specified by the keyword record parameters.

In all variants, a check is then made for additional mortality due to trees reaching a morphological diameter limit entered with the TREESZCP keyword record. This is a user-controlled surrogate for simulating senescence mortality.

When holding SDI to a maximum value, basal area can creep upward. In the SDI-based mortality models a check is made to make sure maximum basal area is still within its’ bound. If stand basal area at this point in subroutine MORTS (i.e. after simulating the mortality thus far) is more than 1 square foot above the maximum basal area specified for the site, the trees per acre attributed to mortality for each tree record is proportionately adjusted upward to bring the maximum basal area back within bounds.

In all variants, subroutine MORTS then calls CLMORTS. CLMORTS determines if any modifications to mortality are needed to account for change in climate. CLMORTS will exist as a subroutine if the climate extension is part of the executable program; it will exist as an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM if the climate extension is not included.

In all variants, subroutine MORTS then utilizes subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND) to find and process any activities scheduled for the projection cycle with the FIXMORT keyword record.

FVS is now done simulating mortality not related to insects, disease, or fire; program control returns to subroutine GRINCR.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine DGBND is called by subroutine REGENT to check for compliance with any morphological maximum tree diameters.

Subroutine DUBSCR is called by subroutine REGENT in some variants to assign a crown ratio to trees larger than 3.0” in diameter.

Subroutine MULTS is used by:

Subroutine DGDRIV to retrieve a flag entered with the MANAGED keyword record indicating the stand should be considered as a “managed stand” for modeling purposes (this affects diameter growth rates in some variants) and any large-tree diameter growth modifiers entered with the BAIMULT keyword record.

Subroutine HTGF to retrieve any large-tree height growth modifiers entered with the HTGMULT keyword record.

Subroutine REGENT to retrieve any small-tree height growth modifiers entered with the REGHMULT keyword record or any small-tree diameter growth modifiers entered with the REGDMULT keyword record.

Subroutine MORTS to retrieve any mortality multipliers entered with the MORTMULT keyword record.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to mark the disposition of growth or mortality activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to see if any growth or mortality activities are scheduled during a projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve parameters associated with any growth or mortality activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

CLGMULT is called by DGDRIV to get a diameter growth multiplier due to climate change. CLGMULT will exist as a subroutine if the climate extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM, which returns a multiplier of 1.0, if the climate extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in section 8.0. They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Record tripling and final adjustments

Following estimation of tree growth and mortality, there are two more tasks that are part of the projection cycling phase. Tree records must be tripled and effects of fertilizer treatments on tree growth must be simulated.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine TRIPLE to triple tree records if record tripling is in effect. Subroutine TRIPLE partitions each tree record into three records. The trees per acre representation of each tree record is computed as described in section 6.4.2 of the EFVS guide. Tree diameter and height growth was tripled in subroutines DGDRIV and REGENT. For each tree record j, subroutine TRIPLE assigns other tree attributes like, species (ISP(j)), trees per acre (PROB(j)), height (HT(j)), crown ratio (ICR(j)), and so forth.

Tripled tree records are added to the internal tree list in sequential order. If the original tree list contained 30 live tree records, then the tripled tree records for the first tree record would be stored as tree records 31 and 32; the second tree record as 33 and 34, …, and the 30th tree record as 89 and 90.

Various FVS extension specific code segments are called by subroutine TRIPLE to triple parameter values associated with the extension. For example, MISGET and MISPUT are called to triple the dwarf mistletoe rating for an individual tree record; and FMTRIP is called to triple snag attributes for the fire and fuels extension. These code segments will exist as subroutines if the extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in the appropriate extension external subroutine (examples are EXMIST for the dwarf mistletoe extension and EXFIRE for the fire and fuels extension) if the extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine REASS to realign the FVS internal pointers following tripling. Subroutine REASS resets the vectors IND(k), IND1(k), and the array ISCT(k1,k2).

Subroutine GRINCR calls subroutine FFERT to compute adjustments to diameter and height growth due to effects of applying fertilizer. Fertilizer treatments can be specified using the FERTILIZ keyword record. With the call to subroutine FFERT in this position, fertilizer treatments do not affect tree mortality through increased competition. This is probably an error but the effects would likely be small. Moving the call to subroutine FFERT before the call to subroutine MORTS should be considered.

Subroutine GRINCR is now done with its’ tasks; program control is returned to subroutine TREGRO for further processing.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to mark the disposition of fertilizer activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to see if any fertilizer activities are scheduled during a projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve parameters associated with any fertilizer activities scheduled during a projection cycle.

Subroutine RCDSET is used by subroutine FFERT to set return codes used by FVS. Return codes are used to signal FVS whether an error was encountered that is significant enough to warrant immediate termination of the projection.

Subroutine SVTRIP is used to adjust the stand visualization file for record tripling.

## Disturbance effects and dynamics

Forest disturbance agents can include insects, diseases, and fire. Dynamics associated with each of these disturbance agents and their effects on tree growth and mortality need to be simulated if those disturbance agents are part of the variant. In addition, some disturbances can be simulated using FVS base model keyword records whether the extension associated with the disturbance agent is part of the variant or not. Lastly, using the stop and restart capabilities, and FVS as a shared library that is called from some other program, disturbances can be modeled outside of FVS and the effects applied using the FVS API calls (see section 8.0).

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine TREGRO calls subroutine GRADD, which among other tasks, checks to see if any of the insect and disease extensions are active. Calls are made to MPBCUP to see if there is a mountain pine beetle outbreak this projection cycle; DFBWIN and DFBDRV for Douglas-fir beetle; MISTOE for dwarf mistletoe; TMCOUP for Douglas-fir tussock moth; BWECUP for western spruce budworm; FMMAIN and FMKILL for the fire and fuels extension; BRTREG for blister rust; RDTREG for western root disease; and BGCFVS for the stand BGC extension. These auxiliary routines will exist as subroutines if the extension is part of the program executable, or entry points in the corresponding externals routine (e.g. subroutine EXRD for western root disease) if the extension in not part of the program executable. These extensions may modify or replace growth and mortality estimates computed previously in the projection cycle by the base FVS subroutines.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine HTGSTP to process any HTGSTOP or FIXHTG keyword records. These keyword records can be used to modify or stop estimated height growth and are useful for simulating effects of disturbance agents such as tussock moth or budworm instead of using the extension itself.

### Auxiliary subroutines

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called by subroutine HTGSTP to mark the disposition of activities associated with the HTGSTOP and FIXHTG keyword records that are scheduled for the current projection cycle.

Subroutine OPFIND is called by subroutine HTGSTP to find activities associated with the HTGSTOP and FIXHTG keyword records that are scheduled for the current projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is called by subroutine HTGSTP to retrieve parameters associated with the HTGSTOP and FIXHTG keyword records that are scheduled for the current projection cycle.

Subroutine OPSTUS is called by subroutine GRADD to check whether conditions under which a fire will be simulated have been set. Fire conditions, such as wind speed, temperature, and fuel moistures, are set using the SIMFIRE keyword record which is specific to the fire and fuels extension. This subroutine checks to see if the activity has been accomplished, deleted, or awaits accomplishment without taking any action to change its status.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in section 8.0. They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Updating the tree descriptions

FVS is now finished with estimation of growth and mortality for the projection cycle. The next tasks are to update the tree descriptions using these estimates, resort the tree records, calculate new stand density statistics, and make any computations needed for the cover extension.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine SVMORT to update the file needed for stand visualization. This update includes the effects of mortality that occurred during the projection cycle. Subroutine SVMORT assumes that all mortality trees are standing snags for purposes of stand visualization. SVMORT calls subroutine SVRMOV to remove tree records associated with mortality (normal, fire-caused, beetle-caused, etc.) from the file needed for stand visualization.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine UPDATE to update tree descriptions. Subroutine UPDATE adds the growth increments, deducts mortality, computes new volume statistics, and calculates some summary information. For each tree record j, updates are made to: tree height, HT(j); normal height, NORMHT(j); trees per acre, PROB(j); and diameter, DBH(j). Tree diameters are updated at the very end of the subroutine, while other values are updated at the beginning of the subroutine. This is because subroutine VOLS, which computes tree volumes, accounts for diameter growth in its calculations.

Subroutine UPDATE updates the array storing mortality-related volume information by tree species and tree value class, SPCMO(sp,vc). It calls subroutine PCTILE to compute percentiles in the distribution of mortality-related volume, and subroutine DIST to compute percentile points in the distribution of mortality-related volume. Subroutine COMP is called to compute percentages of mortality-related volume by species and tree value class.

Subroutine UPDATE calls subroutine VOLS to compute tree and stand volume statistics. It then updates tree diameters and returns control to subroutine GRADD.

Subroutine GRADD needs to recalculate some control and summary variables based on the updated tree records. GRADD calls subroutine RDPSRT to resort the tree records by updated diameter values. It then calls subroutine DENSE to recalculate stand density statistics based on updated trees per acre values.

The next step is dependent on whether the cover extension is part of the variant. Subroutine GRADD calls CVGO to see if the cover extension is active. If it is, then CVBROW is called to compute shrub density and browse statistics. CVGO and CVBROW will exist as subroutines if the cover extension is part of the program executable, or as entry points in subroutine EXCOV if the cover extension is not part of the program executable.

Subroutine GRADD then updates the array containing actual or approximated tree age, ABIRTH(j) for each tree record j.

FVS is now ready to simulate regeneration establishment.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine ECVOL is used to process volume information for the economics post-processor if an economics analysis is called for.

Subroutine VARVOL contains entry points NATCRS, OCFVOL, OBFVOL, and GETEQN. Subroutine VOLS calls entry point NATCRS which calls PROFILE when equations from the National Cruise Program are being used to estimate volumes, or calls other Region specific subroutines (e.g. subroutines FORMCL and R6VOL for Region 6; subroutine R5HARV for Region 5); subroutine VOLS calls entries OCFVOL and OBFVOL or subroutines CFVOL and BFVOL when users change the volume calculation method using field 7 of the VOLUME keyword record. By default, FVS uses the National Cruise Program equations. Entry point GETEQN is used by subroutine NATCRZ to return the volume equation number being used when writing an output file for the National Cruise Program post-processor. Subroutine VOLS calls subroutines CFTOPK and BFTOPK to compute volume lost to broken or dead tops.

Subroutine VOLKEY is called by subroutine VOLS to process any keyword records used to change volume standards or volume equations. These keyword records include MCDEFECT, BFDEFECT, VOLUME, and BFVOLUME.

Subroutines fvsGetRestartCode, getAmStopping, fvsGetRtnCode, and fvsStopPoint (the source code for these subroutines is part of the source code of subroutine CMDLINE) are covered in section 8.0. They are used to control program flow when a stop point is specified.

## Regeneration establishment

The regeneration establishment extension is part of all variants. Regeneration is added near the end of the growth projection cycle. Climate may have an influence on regeneration if the climate extension is also part of the variant. The regeneration establishment extension is described in section 5.4 of the EFVS guide and any variant-specific parameter settings are given in the variant overview documents. Also, section 10.0 of this document presents a more detailed discussion of the regeneration establishment model structure.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine GRADD calls CLAUESTB to determine if any regeneration is occurring because of changes in climate. CLAUESTB will exist as a subroutine if the climate extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXCLIM if the climate extension is not part of the program executable. The climate extension simulates regeneration due to climate change by adding planting activity records (i.e. PLANT keyword records) to the activity list. These planting activities will then get processed when the FVS regeneration establishment model is called at the next step.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine ESNUTR, which is part of the regeneration establishment extension to simulate any regeneration occurring this projection cycle. Regeneration can occur through stump sprouting if a sprouting species was harvested, planting activities scheduled with the PLANT keyword record, or natural regeneration scheduled with the NATURAL keyword record or occurring automatically in some variants.

Regeneration can also be added from an external source using the ADDTREES keyword record. Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESADDT to add trees from an external source.

Parameter settings specified using the SPECMULT, STOCKADJ, and HTADJ keyword records are retrieved and processed with calls to subroutine OPFIND, OPGET (an entry point in subroutine OPFIND), and OPDONE (another entry point in subroutine OPFIND).

#### Stump and root sprouts

Subroutine ESNUTR adds stump sprouts next. This is done in two steps: 1) if necessary, the tree list is compressed so there will be room to add sprouts, and 2) sprouts get added. Sprouting is one form of automatic regeneration that occurs whenever a designated sprouting species is harvested and the user has not turned sprouting off using the NOSPROUT keyword record or the SPROUT keyword record with a multiplier (field 2) of zero.

Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESCPRS to direct compression of the tree list. The tree list must be compressed to about ½ the maximum number of tree records allowed in an FVS projection (parameter MAXTRE in the PRGPRM labeled COMMON block). Subroutine ESCPRS calls subroutines: COMPRS to compress the tree list; SPESRT to reset the species-ordered sort; RDPSRT to reset the diameter sort; PCTILE to reset the distribution of trees per acre and trees per acre by species and tree class; FINDAG to estimate any missing tree ages; DIST to compute diameters corresponding to the nominal percentile points in the distribution of trees per acre; COMP to compute the percentage of trees per acre by species and tree class; and OPADD to add a compression (i.e. COMPRESS keyword record) to the activity schedule and signal the year that it was done.

Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESUCKR to create tree records corresponding to stump and root sprouts from sprouting species harvested at the beginning of a projection cycle. ESUCKR first processes any activities scheduled for the projection cycle using the SPROUT keyword record and stores that information. Next it loops over all tree records for which harvesting occurred and checks to see if the species associated with that tree record is a designated sprouting species for that variant. If it is a sprouting species and sprouting has not been turned off, ESUCKR calls NSPREC, ESASID, and ASSPTN (which are entry points in subroutine ESSPRT) and subroutine ESSPRT to determine the number of sprout records to create for this tree record. The number of sprout records to create will be an integer number. A sub-loop over the number of sprout records to create is then entered to actually create the new sprout records. If subroutine ESUCKR runs out of room to create the necessary sprout records, then another compression of the tree list may become necessary. Subroutine ESUCKR calls SPRTHT, another entry point in subroutine ESSPRT, to determine sprout height which is species and variant dependent. Subroutine ESUCKR calls subroutine CWCALC to calculate crown width and MISPUTZ to initialize the dwarf mistletoe rating for the newly created sprout record to zero. MISPUTZ will exist as a subroutine when the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXMIST when the dwarf mistletoe extension is not part of the program executable. When all harvested tree records have been processed and sprouting has occurred, then a sprouting regeneration report is written and ESUCKR returns program control back to subroutine ESNUTR.

If sprouting has occurred, subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine SPESRT to reset the species order sort, and subroutine RDPSRT to reset pointers in the diameter sort. The variable IFST is set to 1 to signal FVS to select new sample tree records the next time subroutine DIST gets called. New sample tree records are selected whenever the FVS tree list changes due to regeneration.

#### Regeneration tallies

Next, subroutine ESNUTR checks for regeneration tallies. Regeneration tallies may be scheduled automatically by FVS in variants having the full establishment model, or by using the TALLY, TALLYONE, or TALLYTWO keyword records in any variant. A tally sequence is also initiated when an ESTAB keyword record is specified. A detailed description of tally sequences and which kinds of tree records get passed to the FVS tree list at the two kinds of tallies are discussed in section 5.4 of the EFVS guide.

#### Natural regeneration and planted trees

Subroutine ESNUTR calls subroutine ESTAB to add regeneration tree records to the FVS tree list in a tally. Compression of the tree list may be necessary to hold the tree records resulting from a regeneration tally. If less than 30% of the tree list is available (i.e. 30% of MAXTRE), subroutine ESCPRS is called. The tally activity is actually marked as accomplished through a call to OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, before subroutine ESTAB gets called. This is because ESTAB calls OPFIND and nested calls to OPFIND are not allowed in the FVS code (i.e. subroutine ESTAB is being called for a tally “found” by subroutine ESNUTR).

Subroutine ESTAB establishes tree records associated with PLANT and NATURAL keyword records in all variants, and tree records resulting from natural regeneration in variants with the full establishment model. This subroutine is very complex.

4.6.1.3.1 Initialization steps

Initialization of variables and replication of the inventory plots occurs first. The regeneration establishment model creates tree records on 1/300th acre plots. Plots are replicated until at least 50 plots are available so within-stand variations in seedling density, species composition, and heights can be achieved.

Site preparation activities scheduled using the MECHPREP or BURNPREP keyword records are then processed. Subroutine ESTAB calls subroutine ESETPR is called to process these keyword record requests; default probabilities are scheduled by subroutine ESPREP. A site preparation type (none, mechanical, or burn) is assigned randomly to each plot.

Activities associated with any PLANT and NATURAL keyword records are each checked. Unless the number of trees being established by one of these requests is greater than 0.001 trees per acre, the request is “DELETED”.

Sums are accumulated for calculation of shade adjustments. Shading affects the trees per acre representation assigned to regeneration tree records.

4.6.1.3.2 Creating the new tree records

Subroutine ESTAB is now ready to create the new tree records. Triple-nested DO loops are entered with the outside loop being over the number of plots on which regeneration is being simulated; the middle loop over the site preparations (note: the number of plots is replicated for each of the site preparation types); and the inside loop over the number of replications of each plot by site preparation combination.

In variants with the full establishment model, natural regeneration is simulated first within this triple-nested DO loop structure. Natural regeneration is regeneration that comes in automatically following a harvest (called an automatic tally in regeneration establishment jargon) or ingrowth which occurs after the regeneration period has passed. A regeneration period is the number of years during which regeneration becomes established as a result of a disturbance (such as a harvest). Automatic tallies can be turned off using NOAUTALY keyword record; ingrowth can be turned off using the NOINGROW keyword record; both can be turned off using the STOCKADJ keyword record with a probability of stocking set to zero; both, along with stump sprouting, can be turned off using the NOAUTOES keyword record.

To simulate natural regeneration in the full establishment model, first, the probability of stocking is calculated using subroutine ESTOCK. When an actual inventory is used to initiate FVS, the full establishment model adjusts for differences between the actual inventory and the predicted stocking. This feature adjusts the stocking curve (predicted stocking) to coincide with a known reference point (the actual inventory). Next, the probability of advanced, subsequent, and excess species is calculated using subroutines ESPADV, ESPSUB, and ESPXCS, respectively. Third, variables that control creation of the natural regeneration tree records are calculated. This third step is rather involved because of the regeneration establishment rules discussed in section 5.4.1 of the EFVS guide: the number of tree records on a stocked plot is determined using subroutine ESTPP; the number of species on the plot is calculated using subroutine ESNSPE; species which will occupy the plot are designated in array IBEST(i), i = 1 to MAXSP, as a value of 1 if the species is present and 0 if the species will not be present; the first tree of each species is assigned a status of advanced or subsequent using subroutines ESPADV and ESPSUB; heights are then assigned to the tallest trees by species and the advanced or subsequent designation using subroutines ESADVH and ESSUBH, respectively; next, a check is made to make sure there is a non-zero probability of trees which will classified as “excess” trees if a “best” tree of the same species was chosen for the plot. And fourth, the tree records corresponding to natural regeneration are created: tree species and height are assigned to the first tree of each species; and species and heights are assigned to excess trees using subroutine ESXCSH; other variables such as tree age are also assigned.

For all variants, tree records resulting from PLANT or NATURAL keyword records are created next. Tree heights are estimated using subroutine ESSUBH and tree ages are also assigned.

For variants using the full establishment model, the “best” trees get chosen next. Best trees are the two tallest trees regardless of species; the one tallest tree of each additional species represent on the plot; and if four trees have not yet been designated as best trees, then select in order of descending height from any of the remaining trees.

At this point, regeneration tree records in all variants still exist only in the regeneration establishment model extension; they must be “passed” to the FVS tree list. A check is made to make sure there is adequate room in the FVS tree list to handle the incoming tree records from the regeneration establishment model. A call to subroutine ESCPRS compresses the FVS tree list to ½ of its maximum length. Tree records are then passed to the FVS tree list with the full complement of variables assigned (species, trees per acre, diameter, height, etc.).

For all variants, subroutine ESGENT is called to grow the regeneration trees from the time they are 5-years old to the end of the projection cycle. Subroutine ESGENT calls subroutine REGENT, which contains the small tree growth equations, to accomplish this task. Subroutine CWCALC is called to calculate the crown width for seedlings and sprouts. The regeneration summary tables are printed.

After the regeneration summary tables are printed, program control returns to subroutine ESNUTR. ESNUTR calls subroutine RDPSRT to reset the FVS diameter sort of the tree list which now includes regeneration tree records. Program control is returned to subroutine GRADD.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine SVESTB to update files used for stand visualization since the FVS tree list now includes tree records created by the regeneration establishment model. It then calls subroutine DENSE to calculate the post-establishment stand density statistics. This concludes tasks associated with the regeneration establishment extension. Next will be the calculation of crown ratio change.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

Subroutine ESPREP is used to set the default site preparation probabilities (none, mechanical, and burn)

Subroutine ESRANN is used to generate random numbers in the regeneration establishment extension.

ESRNSD, an entry point in subroutine ESRANN, is used to reseed the random number generator in the regeneration establishment extension.

Subroutine ESTIME is used to calculate the time interval between the tally year and the year of disturbance, or site preparation, or the beginning of the current tally.

Subroutine MYOPEN is used to open an external file to be used for regeneration information.

OPDEL1, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to delete an activity scheduled for the projection cycle.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to set the year an activity is accomplished.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to find any regeneration related activities scheduled for the projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve activities and related parameters scheduled for the projection cycle to the subroutine that will process them.

OPGETC, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve a character string associated with an activity.

Subroutine OPRDAT is used to read a file containing activities that need to be scheduled for the current stand.

Subroutine SPESRT is used to reset the species order sort of tree records.

## Computing crown ratio change and crown width

Change in a trees’ crown ratio and a trees’ crown width are the last tree attributes to be estimated during a growth projection cycle. A tree’s crown ratio may decrease, stay the same, or increase. In all variants except IE, and for species in the IE variant that are not one of the original 11 NI variant species, the increase in crown ratio is explicitly bounded to either 1% per year of the growth projection cycle (i.e. 10% for a 10-year cycle), or the amount of change possible if all height growth contributes to crown ratio, whichever is less. For the original 11 NI species in the IE variant the increase is bounded only to 1% per year of the growth projection cycle but the height growth bound is implicit in the logic.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine CROWN to estimate the change in a trees’ crown ratio. In some variants, crown ratio is held constant for trees smaller than a threshold diameter; this is not the case in other variants. Also, this threshold diameter may be species dependent in some of the variants that use it. The three general types of crown ratio models used in FVS are discussed in section 7.4 of the EFVS guide. The logic used in a specific variant is given in each of the variant overview documents. A fourth type, the ORGANON crown ratio model is used in the two ORGANON-FVS variants and discussed in the OC and OP variant overviews. Structural differences in the two ORGANON-FVS variants are further discussed in section 9.0.

Subroutine CROWN uses a nested DO loop structure with the outer loop being over species and the inner loop over tree records of a given species. The coding of subroutine CROWN is straight forward and easy to understand.

Once the end-of-cycle crown ratios have been estimated for all trees, program control returns to subroutine GRADD. If the BGC extension is being used, GRADD calls BGCFVS to replace the crown width values estimated in crown with BGC estimates of crown width. BGCFVS will exist as a subroutine if the BGC extension is part of the program executable or as an entry point in subroutine EXBGC if the extension is not included in the program executable.

Subroutine GRADD calls subroutine CWIDTH to update crown width values for each tree record. Since subroutine CWIDTH doesn’t assign any species-specific constants, a single DO loop is used which loops over all tree records. If a user entered their own crown width equation coefficients using the CWEQN keyword record, subroutine CWIDTH uses these coefficients to estimate crown width. These coefficients are carried in the CWDCOM labeled COMMON block. If the default crown width equations are being used, subroutine CWIDTH calls subroutine CWCALC for each tree record to estimate crown width using individual tree parameters such as species, diameter, height, and crown ratio.

Subroutine CWCALC contains the actual crown width equations. There are two versions of this subroutine: the version used in western variants is stored in the NI variant source directory; the version used in eastern variants is stored in the LS variant source directory. Each crown width equation is numbered. The western version of subroutine CWCALC maps to an equation number based on the variant and species numerical sequence number for that variant; the eastern version of subroutine CWCALC maps to an equation number based on the FVS alpha code for the species.

When crown widths have been updated for all tree records, subroutine CWIDTH returns program control to subroutine GRADD. If the cover extension is active, subroutine GRADD next calls CVCNOP to compute new crown area and foliage biomass estimates. CVCNOP will exist as a subroutine if the cover extension is part of the program executable or as an entry point in subroutine EXCOV if the extension is not included in the program executable. And finally, subroutine GRADD calls subroutines PCTILE, DIST, and COMP to update distributions and percentile points for various attributes that have changed during the projection cycle. Subroutine GRADD returns program control back to subroutine TREGRO.

The growth projection portion of the projection cycle is now complete and subroutine TREGRO passes program control back to subroutine FVS which must now complete the end-of-cycle stand and output table updating.

### Auxiliary subroutines

Subroutine DBCHK is used to see if debug output should be written to the output file.

OPDONE, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to set the year any CRNMULT or FIXCW activities are accomplished.

Subroutine OPFIND is used to find any CRNMULT or FIXCW activities scheduled for the projection cycle.

OPGET, an entry point in subroutine OPFIND, is used to retrieve any CRNMULT or FIXCW activities scheduled for the projection cycle.

Subroutine RANN is used to return a random number in some versions of subroutine CROWN.

## End-Of-Cycle Updating of stand and output information

FVS has several tasks to accomplish at the end of a projection cycle. Output tables must be updated, files used in post-processing programs may need to be written, stand age might need to be reset, and system calls might need to be processed.

### Subroutines involved and their function

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine EXTREE to assign values to the output arrays for example trees. Subscripts to trees used for printing in the output tables are carried in array INS(i), i=1,6, and passed in the CONTRL labeled COMMON block. The INS(i) array is loaded in subroutine DIST.

Subroutine FVS then calls subroutine DISPLY to write the end-of-cycle stand and tree statistics to the stand composition, sample tree, and summary statistics tables. The scalar variable ICL6 is used for various purposes in FVS and is carried in the CONTRL labeled COMMON block. Subroutine DISPLY checks the value of ICL6 to know if the projection is complete (ICL6 < 0) or not (ICL6 > 0). Processing once the projection is complete is discussed in section 5.0.

Subroutine FVS calls subroutine RESAGE to reset the stand age if any RESETAGE keyword records were specified by the user. Users may want to reset the stand age when regeneration or other management activities occur that significantly change the composition of the stand.

Subroutine FVS next calls MISPRT to write end-of-cycle values to dwarf mistletoe summary tables. MISPRT will exist as a subroutine if the dwarf mistletoe extension is part of the program executable, or as an entry point in subroutine EXMIST if the dwarf mistletoe extension in not part of the program executable.

Code segments that write summary output for other insect and disease extensions are called next. These code segments are RDPR for the western root disease model and BRPR for the blister rust model. RDPR and BRPR will exist as subroutines if the extension is part of the program executable or as an entry point in the corresponding externals subroutine if it is not.
